A 66 year old gentleman, who is a known heavy smoker, presents with a
non infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD). Upon admission despite maximal medical therapy his blood
gasses worsen and he is commenced on non invasive ventilation and
transferred to the high dependency unit. The nurses call you in the
middle of the night to come and urgently review the patient. They have
been titrating up the patient's non invasive ventilation (NIV) as they felt
his blood gasses were not improving on standard settings. On arrival the
patient is diaphoretic and complaining of chest pain. He is unable to
tolerate his face mask. Observations are recorded as a pulse of 110/min
regular, respiratory rate 32/min, Sats 75% on air, Blood pressure 100/82
mmHg. What is the most likely cause for this patient's acute
deterioration?
Ventilator associated pneumonia
Acute myocardial infarction
Ventilator associated pneumothorax
Worsening of his COPD
Panic attack

A 66 year old gentleman, who is a known heavy smoker, presents with a
non infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD). Upon admission despite maximal medical therapy his blood
gasses worsen and he is commenced on non invasive ventilation and
transferred to the high dependency unit. The nurses call you in the
middle of the night to come and urgently review the patient. They have
been titrating up the patient's non invasive ventilation (NIV) as they felt
his blood gasses were not improving on standard settings. On arrival the
patient is diaphoretic and complaining of chest pain. He is unable to
tolerate his face mask. Observations are recorded as a pulse of 110/min
regular, respiratory rate 32/min, Sats 75% on air, Blood pressure 100/82
mmHg. What is the most likely cause for this patient's acute
deterioration?
explanation:
This question assesses candidates ability to recognise some of the
complications of NIV. This patient has developed a pneumothorax
secondary to the increasing pressures used as part of his NIV. Although
less common these days due to nurse training, ventilation associated
pneumothorax is an important complication of NIV to be aware of and
therefore, prompt assessment and treatment will be essential in the
management of this patient.
Ventilator associated pneumonia tends to present in patients who have
been ventilated for long a long period of time and would not present so
acutely.
Acute myocardial infarction would be unlikely as the question makes a
point of mentioning the increasing pressures that are needed.
Candidates should also familiarise themselves with some of the
contraindications to NIV:
- Recent facial or upper airway surgery or facial injuries.
- Recent upper gastrointestinal surgery.
- Confusion/agitation.
- Bowel obstruction.
- Upper airway obstruction.
- Excessive upper airway secretions.
- Patient actively vomiting.
May of these are self explanatory, for a more comprehensive list,
including the indications for use of NIV please visit:
thoracic.org.uk/document-library/clinical-information/niv/niv-
guidelines/nippv-non-invasive-ventilation-in-acute-respiratory-failure/
Non-invasive ventilation
The British Thoracic Society (BTS) published guidelines in 2002 on the
use of non-invasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure. Following
these the Royal College of Physicians published guidelines in 2008.
Non-invasive ventilation - key indications
COPD with respiratory acidosis pH 7.25-7.35
the BTS guidelines state that NIV can be used in patients who
are more acidotic (i.e. pH < 7.25) but that a greater degree of
monitoring is required (e.g. HDU) and a lower threshold for
intubation and ventilation should be used

A 69-year-old man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis well controlled
on methotrexate presents with gradual pain and swelling in his wrists
and ankles.
The pain is described as a dull ache that is intermittent, often worse in
the evenings. There is associated swelling which can sometimes feel
warm. He has tried regular paracetamol but this has had limited effect.
He also describes a chronic cough and shortness of breath on exertion
for the past 6 months that he has not mentioned to his GP. There has
been no haemoptysis and he denies any fevers. His wife has noticed that
he has been losing weight recently.
He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension,
hypercholesterolaemia and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He currently takes
methotrexate weekly, folic acid 5mg weekly, ramipril 5mg, simvastatin
20mg at night, metformin 500mg three times a day and paracetamol 1g

He is a retired accountant and a current smoker with a 50 pack year

denies any recent foreign travel.
On examination, he is cachectic and short of breath on exertion. His
pulse is 80/min and regular, blood pressure 140/93 mmHg, oxygen

Examination of his wrists reveals slightly swollen and tender joints.

explanation:
The chest x-ray shows cannonball metastases which are most
commonly caused by renal cell cancer. A CT abdomen is the most
appropriate test to investigate this possibility.
Other tests should of course be considered including a prostate specific
antigen.

This depends on the clinical context, but is usually 2cm laterally or
Chest drain insertion is the most appropriate management for this
patient. According to the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2023 guidelines
for spontaneous pneumothorax, the management approach depends on
whether the patient is symptomatic and if high-risk characteristics are
present. This patient is clearly symptomatic with chest pain, shortness
of breath, tachypnoea (respiratory rate 24), and reduced oxygen
saturation (92%). Additionally, he has multiple high-risk characteristics
including age over 50 years with a significant smoking history (40 pack-
years) and underlying lung disease (COPD). The guidelines specifically
recommend chest drain insertion for symptomatic patients with high-
risk characteristics, provided it is safe to intervene. In this case, with
3cm of air visible laterally on chest X-ray, intervention is considered safe
(the guideline threshold is typically 2cm laterally or apically on chest X-
ray). The presence of COPD makes this a secondary spontaneous
pneumothorax, which carries higher risks and typically requires more
aggressive management than primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Conservative management with outpatient follow-up would be
inappropriate for this patient. Conservative management is
recommended for patients with no or minimal symptoms, regardless of
pneumothorax size. This patient is clearly symptomatic with respiratory
distress and has high-risk features including COPD and age over 50 with
significant smoking history. Additionally, while primary spontaneous
pneumothorax patients managed conservatively can be reviewed as
outpatients every 2-4 days, secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
patients (like this one with COPD) should be monitored as inpatients if
managed conservatively.
Needle aspiration is not the first-line treatment for patients with
symptomatic pneumothorax and high-risk characteristics. While needle
aspiration may be considered for symptomatic patients without high-risk
characteristics, this patient has multiple high-risk features (age >50 with
smoking history and COPD). The BTS guidelines recommend proceeding
directly to chest drain insertion in such cases.
Insertion of an ambulatory device such as a Rocket Pleural Vent might
apically on chest x-ray, or any size on CT scan which can be safely
accessed with radiological support
be considered for some patients with pneumothorax, but it is not the
first-line recommendation for patients with high-risk characteristics
according to the BTS guidelines. This patient's age, underlying COPD,
and significant smoking history make chest drain insertion the preferred
option to ensure adequate lung re-expansion and monitoring.
Immediate referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
would be premature at this stage. VATS is typically considered for
patients with persistent air leak or insufficient lung re-expansion despite
chest drain insertion, or for those with recurrent pneumothoraces. This
patient is presenting with his first episode (as far as we know from the
scenario) and has not yet had a trial of chest drain management. VATS
would be considered if the pneumothorax persists despite appropriate
initial management with a chest drain.

A 71-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden
onset left-sided chest pain and mild breathlessness. He has a history of
COPD and a 50 pack-year smoking history. On examination, he is
comfortable at rest, with oxygen saturations of 96% on room air,
respiratory rate 18/min, heart rate 82 bpm and blood pressure 134/78
mmHg. Chest auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds on the left
side. A chest X-ray confirms a moderate left-sided pneumothorax. The
patient reports only minimal discomfort and no significant
breathlessness at rest. After multidisciplinary discussion, a decision is
made for conservative management.
What is the most appropriate next step in his care?
Admit for inpatient observation
Discharge with outpatient review in 2–4 days
Insert ambulatory pleural vent device and discharge
Perform needle aspiration in the emergency department
Arrange urgent surgical referral
Question 29 of 241
A 71-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden
onset left-sided chest pain and mild breathlessness. He has a history of
COPD and a 50 pack-year smoking history. On examination, he is
comfortable at rest, with oxygen saturations of 96% on room air,
respiratory rate 18/min, heart rate 82 bpm and blood pressure 134/78
mmHg. Chest auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds on the left
side. A chest X-ray confirms a moderate left-sided pneumothorax. The
patient reports only minimal discomfort and no significant
breathlessness at rest. After multidisciplinary discussion, a decision is
made for conservative management.
What is the most appropriate next step in his care?
options: Discharge with outpatient review in 2–4 days
Insert ambulatory pleural vent device and discharge
Perform needle aspiration in the emergency department
explanation:
Admit for inpatient observation is correct because this patient has a
secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) due to underlying COPD
and age over 50 with significant smoking history—both high-risk features
per BTS guidelines. Even though he is minimally symptomatic and
conservative management is chosen, the BTS 2023 guidelines
Patients with a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax that is
managed conservatively should be monitored as an inpatient
recommend that patients with SSP managed conservatively should be
admitted for inpatient monitoring rather than discharged home. This
allows close observation for potential deterioration or development of
complications such as worsening hypoxia or tension physiology.
Discharge with outpatient review in 2–4 days would be appropriate if
this were a primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) managed
conservatively; however, SSP patients require more careful monitoring
due to their increased risk of clinical deterioration even when initially
stable. Outpatient follow-up alone does not provide adequate safety
netting for these higher-risk individuals.
Insert ambulatory pleural vent device and discharge may be considered
in selected cases of PSP or less frail SSP patients who are symptomatic
but do not have high-risk characteristics, provided it can be done safely
and there are robust systems for follow-up. However, current UK
guidance recommends caution using ambulatory devices in older adults
with comorbidities like COPD; furthermore, as this patient’s symptoms
are minimal, conservative management (not intervention) was already
agreed upon.
Perform needle aspiration in the emergency department could be
considered if the patient were more symptomatic or had failed
conservative management; however, as he only has minimal symptoms
and no physiological compromise, immediate intervention is not
indicated according to BTS recommendations.
Arrange urgent surgical referral would be necessary if there was
evidence of persistent air leak after chest drain insertion or
recurrent/persistent pneumothoraces despite appropriate initial
management. In this scenario, neither applies: this is an initial
presentation being managed conservatively without evidence that
surgery is currently needed.

What is the most likely explanation of the failure to improve?
explanation:
The patient has a clear COPD exacerbation and starts non invasive
ventilation but fails to improve. The clues are the audible hiss of air that
can be heard from the mask and the failure of the machine to achieve
the pressures set. Poor mask application or facial dysmorphia can lead
to a poor seal to the face. Air will leak and the pressure will fall with this.
The patient is unlikely to have deteriorated due to reducing
consciousness secondary to CO2 narcosis as he continues to breathe at
an elevated respiratory rate. There is no suggestion of a pneumothorax
and this usually presents as a deterioration rather than a failure to
improve. The patient is comfortable and does not appear to be fighting
the machine as in dyssynchrony. A large mucus plug usually presents
with sudden desaturation which is not seen here.
Significant air leak from the mask will prevent adequate pressures
being achieved with non-invasive ventilation

on exertion. He has had the cough for over 2 years, but it has gotten
worse recently along with increasing shortness of breath. He has no
haemoptysis, chest pain or leg swelling. The patient has a 60 pack-year
smoking history and drinks a moderate amount of alcohol. His
temperature is 37.2ºC, blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg, pulse is 80/min,
and respirations are 20/min.
Chest x-ray shows prominent bronchovascular markings and mild
diaphragmatic flattening.

A 60-year-old man comes to his GP complaining of cough and dyspnoea
on exertion. He has had the cough for over 2 years, but it has gotten
worse recently along with increasing shortness of breath. He has no
haemoptysis, chest pain or leg swelling. The patient has a 60 pack-year
smoking history and drinks a moderate amount of alcohol. His
temperature is 37.2ºC, blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg, pulse is 80/min,
and respirations are 20/min.
Chest x-ray shows prominent bronchovascular markings and mild
diaphragmatic flattening.
Pulmonary function test results are as follows:
Forced expiratory volume in 1 second
67% of predicted
Forced vital capacity
95% of predicted
FEV1/FVC ratio
0.65
Carbon monoxide diffusion capacity is 100% of predicted value.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patients
symptoms?
explanation:
The patients pulmonary function test (PFT) findings are consistent with
obstructive lung disease. The carbon monoxide diffusing capacity of the
lung (DLCO) measures the lungs ability to transfer gas to the blood. This
patients normal DLCO indicates intact alveolar and capillary structure.
The patients chronic smoking, productive cough, dyspnoea on exertion
and decreased FEV1/FVC ratio suggests COPD. COPD is a group of
chronic disorders; the main subtypes being emphysema or chronic
bronchitis. Patients with predominant emphysema are generally thin
with severe dyspnoea, hyperinflated chest, decreased vascular markings,
decreased DLCO (due to alveolar destruction) and moderate oxygen
desaturation.
Patients with predominant chronic bronchitis have chronic productive
cough for 3 months over 2 consecutive years not due to other causes
(e.g. bronchiectasis). It usually presents with prominent bronchovascular
markings, mildly flattened diaphragm and normal DLCO (as seen in this
patient).

explanation:
This patient has presented with features of eosinophilic pneumonia
secondary to parasite infection, also known as Loefflers syndrome. The
most likely causative organism in this case is the roundworm Ascaris
lumbricoides, which can cause Loefflers syndrome during the pulmonary
migration phase of its life cycle. The clinical features and eosinophilia
could also point to idiopathic pulmonary eosinophilia or allergic
bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, but the treatment for both of these
(corticosteroids) is not listed as a potential answer. The chest x-ray
findings and normal ECG make pulmonary embolism a less likely
diagnosis.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA, also known as hypersensitivity
pneumonitis) is a condition caused by hypersensitivity induced lung
damage due to a variety of inhaled organic particles. It is thought to be
largely caused by immune-complex mediated tissue damage (type III
hypersensitivity) although delayed hypersensitivity (type IV) is also
thought to play a role in EAA, especially in the chronic phase.
Examples
bird fanciers' lung: avian proteins from bird droppings
farmers lung: spores of Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula from wet hay

doxazosin and gliclazide.
On examination, he is comfortable on lying flat but is noticeably
dyspnoeic when mobilising. He has minimal ankle oedema, his heart rate
is 78 beats per minute and he has fine bibasal crepitations on
auscultation of his chest. His oxygen saturations on air are 92%.
An echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%, a
mildly hypertrophied left ventricle and well established right ventricular
hypertrophy, pulmonary artery pressures are raised at 32 mmHg (normal:

A 68-year-old is seen in a cardiology clinic. He has a part history of long-
standing atrial fibrillation, hypertension and ischaemic heart disease. He
describes progressive shortness of breath over the past year and a dry
cough. His medication history includes aspirin, amiodarone, ramipril,
doxazosin and gliclazide.
On examination, he is comfortable on lying flat but is noticeably
dyspnoeic when mobilising. He has minimal ankle oedema, his heart rate
is 78 beats per minute and he has fine bibasal crepitations on
auscultation of his chest. His oxygen saturations on air are 92%.
An echocardiogram reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%, a
mildly hypertrophied left ventricle and well established right ventricular
hypertrophy, pulmonary artery pressures are raised at 32 mmHg (normal:
< 25 mmHg). A chest x-ray shows non-specific changes on both bases.
What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
The raised pulmonary artery pressures and right ventricular hypertrophy
points to a respiratory pathology. Despite the history of atrial fibrillation a
cardiac cause is less likely to be causing his dyspnoea in view of the fact
that he is comfortable when lying flat (i.e. no orthopnoea), he has
minimal ankle oedema and that his left ventricular function is only mildly
impaired. This patient should be investigated for interstitial lung disease
in view of his history of amiodarone use. In light of this an exercise
stress test, a cardiac MRI and a repeat echo are unlikely to be of any
benefit and there is no indication to perform overnight oximetry. An
HRCT is warranted to help aid establish a diagnosis.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

A 57-year-old woman is admitted with an infective exacerbation of
bronchiectasis. Multiple sputum cultures in the community have grown
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and her GP had started oral ciprofloxacin.
However, despite 4 days of this, she has developed worsening
breathlessness, hypoxia, and fever and is now requiring oxygen.
Widespread coarse crepitations are heard and her chest x-ray
demonstrates bilateral infiltrates.
What is the most appropriate course of action?
Add IV clarithromycin
Add IV vancomycin
Add high-dose trimethoprim/sulphamethoxazole and
prednisolone
Change to IV ertapenem
Change to IV piperacillin-tazobactam
Question 136 of 140
A 57-year-old woman is admitted with an infective exacerbation of
bronchiectasis. Multiple sputum cultures in the community have grown
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and her GP had started oral ciprofloxacin.
However, despite 4 days of this, she has developed worsening
breathlessness, hypoxia, and fever and is now requiring oxygen.
Widespread coarse crepitations are heard and her chest x-ray
demonstrates bilateral infiltrates.
What is the most appropriate course of action?
explanation:
The correct answer is change to IV piperacillin-tazobactam.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a recognised cause of complex respiratory
tract infections in patients with bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis. Where
oral treatment with ciprofloxacin fails, options include IV piperacillin-
tazobactam, ceftazidime, or meropenem.
Appropriate treatment of Pseudomonas positive bronchiectasis
failing to respond to ciprofloxacin includes IV tazocin, ceftazidime,
aztreonam or meropenem
Add IV clarithromycin is incorrect. This is active against common
pathogens causing community-acquired pneumonia as well as some
atypical organisms. However, in this case, an organism has been
isolated and it would be more appropriate to convert to IV therapy active
against this. The combination of clarithromycin with quinolones also
increases the risk of QT interval prolongation.
Add IV vancomycin is incorrect. This has purely gram-positive cover and
is not active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Add high-dose trimethoprim/sulphamethoxazole and prednisolone is
incorrect. This would be the optimal treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii
which can cause severe bilateral pneumonia. However, it is most
commonly seen as an opportunistic infection in patients with impaired
cell-mediated immunity, classically patients with HIV infection. In this
case, there is no suggestion of significant immunocompromise and a
typical pathogen has been isolated. It is therefore more appropriate to
target therapy against this organism.
Change to IV ertapenem is incorrect. Ertapenem is a carbapenem (the
same class as meropenem) with extremely broad-spectrum
antimicrobial activity. However, the main difference between ertapenem
and meropenem is that the former lacks activity against Pseudomonas
species. It would therefore not be effective in this case.

rural Southeast Asia. He denies fever, weight loss, or haemoptysis. Chest
auscultation reveals scattered wheezes. A chest X-ray shows transient,

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Löffler’s syndrome is the correct answer. The patient presents with the
classic triad of Löffler's syndrome: mild respiratory symptoms (dry
cough and mild dyspnoea), transient peripheral pulmonary infiltrates on
chest imaging, and marked peripheral eosinophilia (3.1×10⁹/L). Recent
travel to rural Southeast Asia, endemic for Ascaris, hookworms, and
Strongyloides, and an elevated IgE level (480 IU/mL) support a parasitic
aetiology. Symptoms are mild and infiltrates are fleeting, resolving
spontaneously as larvae complete their transpulmonary migration. The
wheezing observed is typically due to the inflammatory response in the
airways triggered by the presence of larvae, not asthma.
After ingestion of parasite eggs (such as Ascaris lumbricoides), larvae
hatch in the intestine, penetrate the intestinal wall, and travel via the
bloodstream to the lungs. They migrate from pulmonary capillaries
through alveolar walls, ascend the bronchial tree, and are swallowed,
returning to the intestine. This transpulmonary passage triggers a T-cell-
dependent hypersensitivity reaction, characterised by IL-5 production,
which leads to eosinophil accumulation in lung tissue and the
development of characteristic pulmonary infiltrates.
Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP) is unlikely in this case because
patients with AEP typically present with more severe, rapidly progressive
respiratory symptoms that can lead to respiratory failure within days.
The patient's mild symptoms over 5 days, absence of fever, and lack of
bilateral diffuse infiltrates make AEP less probable. Additionally, AEP
often presents initially with normal or only mildly elevated peripheral
eosinophil counts, unlike the marked eosinophilia seen in this patient.
The chest imaging in AEP typically shows bilateral, diffuse ground-glass
opacities rather than the unilateral, fleeting peripheral infiltrates
described here.
Drug-induced eosinophilic pneumonia is implausible in this scenario.
Drug reactions, such as those caused by NSAIDs and antibiotics, involve
elevated IgE and a clear temporal link to medication use. This patient
denies recent drug exposure, which excludes this possibility.
CXR shadowing and eosinophilia → ?Loffler's syndrome
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is incorrect. ABPA
characteristically presents with central bronchiectasis on chest imaging
rather than peripheral infiltrates. Whilst the elevated IgE could support
ABPA, the patient's travel history to an area endemic for parasites and
the pattern of fleeting peripheral infiltrates are more consistent with
parasitic-induced eosinophilia.
Mycoplasma pneumonia is incorrect. While it shares the same
presentation in the case (fatigue, dry cough, and mild dyspnoea) and
radiographic findings can be non-specific, Mycoplasma infection doesn't
typically cause significant eosinophilia. The patient's marked
eosinophilia makes this diagnosis unlikely.
Pulmonary eosinophilia
Pulmonary eosinophilia describes a situation where there are increased
numbers of eosinophils in the lung airways and parenchyma. This is
generally associated with a blood eosinophilia.
Causes of pulmonary eosinophilia
Churg-Strauss syndrome
allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)
Loffler's syndrome
eosinophilic pneumonia
hypereosinophilic syndrome
tropical pulmonary eosinophilia
drugs: nitrofurantoin, sulphonamides
less common: Wegener's granulomatosis
Loffler's syndrome
transient CXR shadowing and blood eosinophilia
thought to be due to parasites such as Ascaris lumbricoides causing
an alveolar reaction

A 71-year-old man is being treated in a medical ward for an empyema.
Shortly after admission, a chest drain is inserted under ultrasound
guidance and antibiotics are started. Over the past few days, there have
been significant volumes drained and the patient has been improving
clinically.
On the daily morning ward round, his chest drain is reviewed. It is on
suction. There is minimal drain output over the past 24 hours and it is
noted that the chest drain is bubbling. This bubbling is more significant
when the patient is asked to cough.
What does this indicate?
Blocked chest drain
Bronchopleural fistula
Chest drain moved displaced outside of the chest
Normal
Unresolved empyema
Question 70 of 241
A 71-year-old man is being treated in a medical ward for an empyema.
Shortly after admission, a chest drain is inserted under ultrasound
guidance and antibiotics are started. Over the past few days, there have
been significant volumes drained and the patient has been improving
clinically.
On the daily morning ward round, his chest drain is reviewed. It is on
suction. There is minimal drain output over the past 24 hours and it is
noted that the chest drain is bubbling. This bubbling is more significant
when the patient is asked to cough.
What does this indicate?
options: Chest drain moved displaced outside of the chest
explanation:
Bubbling of a chest drain inserted into the pleural space is indicative of
an air leak. Therefore, given the clinical history of an empyema, it is likely
that a bronchopleural fistula has formed. This is therefore the correct
answer.
As there is bubbling of the chest drain, it cannot be blocked. This is
Bubbling of a chest drain inserted to drain an empyema may
indicates that a bronchopleural fistula has occurred
therefore an incorrect answer.
If the chest drain is displaced outside of the chest and on suction,
bubbling can occur. Distinguishing between a bronchopleural fistula and
a displaced chest drain can be difficult however one simple test is to ask
the patient to cough. As the patient coughs and the intrathoracic
pressure rises, this will cause an increase in the air flowing into the
pleural space and therefore the bubbling of the drain. If the drain is
outside of the pleural space, the bubbling will be constant and unrelated
to coughing.
Bubbling from a chest drain is not a normal finding . Although swinging
is normal with changes in intrathoracic pressure, bubbling is caused by
air being entrained into the drain. The most common cause for this is the
displacement of the drain outside of the thorax, however, a
bronchopleural fistula is the diagnosis here as indicated by the changes
on coughing.
An unresolved empyema is not necessarily indicated here by the drain
activity as this would not cause bubbling of the chest drain. The drain is
clearly patent, as indicated by the bubbling which is worse on coughing,
and there is minimal drain output. It may be that the drain is not located
within the empyema limiting its resolution, however further imaging
would be required to determine this.
Chest drain
A chest drain is a tube inserted into the pleural cavity which creates a
one-way valve, allowing movement of air or liquid out of the cavity.
Chest drain insertion is indicated in cases of:
Pleural effusion
Pneumothorax not suitable for conservative management or
aspiration

Question 82 of 241
A 76-year-old retired boiler engineer presents with a 3-week history of a
cough following a coryzal illness. He was a heavy smoker until around
five years ago. An x-ray is performed:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What does the chest x-ray demonstrate?
explanation:
The correct answer is Pleural plaques. Pleural plaques are areas of
fibrous thickening on the pleura (the lining of the lungs) and are often
associated with exposure to asbestos. They are usually asymptomatic
and do not typically affect lung function. The chest x-ray in the question
shows bilateral pleural thickening, which is characteristic of pleural
plaques. Their presence can indicate past exposure to asbestos, which
would be consistent with the patient's history as a boiler engineer.
The first incorrect option is Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD). Although the patient has a history of heavy smoking, which is a
leading risk factor for COPD, this condition would not typically manifest
as pleural plaques on an x-ray. Instead, one might expect to see
hyperinflation of the lungs or potentially bullae (areas of
emphysematous change), neither of which are evident in this image.
Next, we have Bronchiectasis, another incorrect choice. Bronchiectasis
refers to permanent enlargement and damage to the airways (bronchi),
often caused by recurrent infection or inflammation. On an x-ray,
bronchiectasis may present as ring-like or tram-line shadows due to
abnormally dilated bronchi; however, these signs are not visible in this
case.
Asbestosis is also suggested but it is not correct either. Asbestosis
refers specifically to interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of
asbestos fibres. While it shares a common cause with pleural plaques
(asbestos exposure), its radiographic appearance differs significantly.
Asbestosis typically presents as small irregular opacities predominantly
in lower lobes and subpleural areas, rather than the discrete areas of
pleural thickening seen here.
Lastly, Lung cancer was proposed as an option but it too does not fit
with the findings on this x-ray. Lung cancers can take various forms on
imaging - from solitary pulmonary nodules to larger masses - but they
generally do not appear as bilateral pleural thickening like that seen in
this image.

A 51-year-old woman is being investigated by the respiratory team. She
reports a four-month history of dry cough with associated lethargy and
weight loss. She has no relevant past medical history and has never
smoked.
A chest x-ray is displayed below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
Which further test would be most appropriate to aid in diagnosis?
Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA)
Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA)
Perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA)
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
Sputum microscopy, culture, and sensitivity (MCS)
Question 39 of 241
A 51-year-old woman is being investigated by the respiratory team. She
reports a four-month history of dry cough with associated lethargy and
weight loss. She has no relevant past medical history and has never
smoked.
A chest x-ray is displayed below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
Which further test would be most appropriate to aid in diagnosis?
explanation:
This woman has sarcoidosis. This explains her clinical symptoms and is
confirmed by the bilateral lymphadenopathy on her chest x-ray. Serum
ACE is a specific blood biomarker for sarcoidosis and is, therefore, the
correct answer in this instance.
cANCA is a biochemical marker for granulomatosis with polyangiitis
(previously known as Wegner's granulomatosis). This classically
presents with haemoptysis, rhinitis, epistaxis, and potentially renal
involvement. The typical x-ray findings include nodules with or without
cavitations, pulmonary haemorrhages, and peripheral consolidation. As
none of these symptoms or imaging features are to be found in this
case, this is not the diagnosis and therefore pANCA is incorrect.
IGRA is a test used to diagnose tuberculosis (TB) infection. Although the
symptoms here could be indicative of active pulmonary TB, this
classically presents with upper lobe consolidation on chest x-ray. As this
is not present, TB is not the diagnosis here. Therefore an IGRA would not
be an appropriate test to order in this instance.
pANCA is a biochemical marker for eosinophilic granulomatosis with
polyangiitis (previously known as Churg-Strauss syndrome). This
typically presents with asthmatic features as well as other sequelae of
vasculitis. The x-ray findings in eosinophilic granulomatosis with
polyangiitis include peripheral consolidation and pleural effusions. As
none of these symptoms or imaging features are to be found in this
case, this is not the diagnosis and therefore pANCA is incorrect.
The x-ray here shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy rather than focal
areas of consolidation and is, therefore, more indicative of sarcoidosis.
Sputum MCS is very effective in identifying organisms and assessing
sensitivities in infective pathologies however have no role in sarcoidosis
as this is an autoimmune process. This is therefore an incorrect answer.

A 35-year-old man who lives in long-term residential care presents with
drowsiness and increased respiratory effort. There is new consolidation
on his chest x-ray and he is diagnosed with pneumonia. His care workers
reported that he had some vomiting episodes 5 days previously.
A sputum sample is analysed in the microbiology laboratory. On
microscopy of the sample, a mixture of Gram-positive cocci and Gram-
negative rods is visible. At 48 hours there is growth on both the blood
agar plate and the anaerobic agar plate.
What finding on sputum culture would provide evidence that his
pneumonia is due to aspiration?
Bacteria which are sensitive to metronidazole
Bacteria which are sensitive to optochin
Bacteria which are sensitive to penicillin
Catalase negative organisms
Growth of Gram negative cocci
Question 83 of 241
A 35-year-old man who lives in long-term residential care presents with
drowsiness and increased respiratory effort. There is new consolidation
on his chest x-ray and he is diagnosed with pneumonia. His care workers
reported that he had some vomiting episodes 5 days previously.
A sputum sample is analysed in the microbiology laboratory. On
microscopy of the sample, a mixture of Gram-positive cocci and Gram-
negative rods is visible. At 48 hours there is growth on both the blood
agar plate and the anaerobic agar plate.
What finding on sputum culture would provide evidence that his
pneumonia is due to aspiration?
options: Bacteria which are sensitive to metronidazole
Bacteria which are sensitive to optochin
Bacteria which are sensitive to penicillin
explanation:
Anaerobic bacteria often contribute to aspiration pneumonia as these
bacteria are part of the microflora of the mouth and digestive tract, and
may enter the respiratory system via aspiration of oral or gastrointestinal
fluids. They are commonly found to cause infection alongside other
aerobic bacteria. It is important to consider whether a patient's
pneumonia may be due to aspiration, as not all the commonly used
antibiotic options for community-acquired pneumonia will treat
Anaerobic bacteria in sputum culture suggest aspiration pneumonia
anaerobic infections.
Most anaerobic bacteria are sensitive to metronidazole, and conversely,
metronidazole does not have any activity against non-anaerobes.
Therefore the presence of metronidazole-sensitive organisms suggests
that there are anaerobes present, which are often found in aspiration
pneumonia.
Optochin is used as a test to differentiate Streptococcus pneumoniae
from other alpha-haemolytic Streptococci. Strep pneumoniae is a
common cause of community-acquired pneumonia and would not
suggest aspiration pneumonia.
Most anaerobic bacteria are not sensitive to penicillin (with a few
exceptions). A penicillin-sensitive organism grown from sputum would
be most likely to be a typical organism such as Strep pneumoniae.
The catalase test is used to differentiate Gram-positive cocci into
Staphylococci or Streptococci. Streptococci are catalase negative.
The most important Gram-negative cocci are Neisseria and Moraxella.
Moraxella catarrhalis can cause respiratory tract infections but is not
associated with aspiration pneumonia.
Aspiration pneumonia
Aspiration pneumonia is a pneumonia that develops as a result of
foreign materials gaining entry to the bronchial tree, usually oral or
gastric contents such as food and saliva. Depending on the acidity of the
aspirate a chemical pneumonitis can develop, as well as bacterial
pathogens adding to the inflammation.
Aspiration pneumonia often results from an incompetent swallowing
mechanism, such as those that occur in neurological disease or injury

characterized by marked deposition of immunoglobulin and
complement. C4 would be markedly low in 90% of patients due to
classical pathway activation by cryoglobulins. This is in contrast to MPA
where the complement levels would be normal or even elevated as an
acute phase response.

explanation:

Whilst the causative organism could potentially be either tuberculosis or
non-tuberculosis mycobacterial (NTM) infection, the latter is the more
appropriate here given the radiological findings on HRCT, which are
classically seen in atypical mycobacterial infection. This question tests

tuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) infection in immunocompetent
individuals. NTM infection in the non-HIV population is becoming
increasingly common and is often a challenging diagnosis to make due
to the environmental nature of NTM.
Nontuberculous mycobacteria
Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are mycobacterial species other
than those belonging to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. NTM
are typically free-living organisms that are common in the environment.
Most non-tuberculous mycobacteria are caused by M. avium complex
(MAC) organisms.
Presentations include:
pulmonary disease
cavitating lesions
nodular / bronchiectatic disease
disseminated disease

The patient in question suffers from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
(usually interstitial pneumonia type) as evident by the restrictive pattern,
lack of history suggestive of other causes of fibrosis alongside the

the pharmacological management of this disease bearing in mind its
irreversible nature.
Pirfenidone and nintedanib are two antifibrotic agents currently licensed
for use in the UK provided the forced vital capacity (FVC) between 50%
and 80% predicted given the evidence in literature currently.
Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5-inhibitor that has been trialled in
such patients in order to examine the potential of improved oxygen
delivery; a study in 2010 concluded that there was no potential benefit in
the use of sildenafil in such patients, except where pulmonary
hypertension exists.
Prednisolone and steroid use in patients with idiopathic pulmonary
fibrosis as a disease modifier has not been proven to be beneficial.
Bosentan is a dual endothelin receptor antagonist that is currently
licensed for the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension. As per the
BUILD-3 trial, the use of bosentan does not delay idiopathic pulmonary
fibrosis progression or death.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

explanation:
Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is correct. Key features pointing to
AAT deficiency:
• Basal-predominant panlobular emphysema (typical of AAT deficiency,
in contrast to centrilobular emphysema seen in smokers).
• Liver dysfunction (AAT deficiency can cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis,
and hepatocellular carcinoma).
• Non-smoker with significant emphysema.
• Family history may reveal liver or lung disease in relatives.
Important next steps would be measuring serum AAT levels and
performing genetic testing for PiZZ genotype.
Alcohol related liver disease is incorrect. Alcoholic liver disease
presents with elevated AST > ALT (often AST: ALT ratio > 2),
macrocytosis, and a history of alcohol excess. It does also not explain
the obstructive pattern seen on spirometry.
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis causes iron
overload, leading to cirrhosis, diabetes (“bronze diabetes”), arthropathy,
and cardiomyopathy. Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation would be
elevated in haemochromatosis, but are not mentioned here. It does not
cause basal emphysema.
Primary biliary cholangitis is incorrect. PBC is a chronic autoimmune
cholestatic liver disease primarily affecting middle-aged women, often
30-40 year old with basal emphysema and abnormal LFTs → ?
alpha-1 antitrypsin
the patient's autoimmune liver screen has returned negative.
Wilson's disease is incorrect. Wilson’s disease causes copper
accumulation, leading to liver disease, neuropsychiatric symptoms
(tremors, dysarthria, dystonia), and Kayser-Fleischer rings. This patient
has no neurological symptoms or haemolysis, and Wilson’s disease is
more common in younger patients (< 40 years). Serum caeruloplasmin
and 24-hour urinary copper excretion would help confirm/exclude the
diagnosis. Again, it would also not explain the obstructive pattern
spirometry results, which clinch the diagnosis of Alpha 1 antitrypsin
deficiency.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1 antitrypsin (A1AT) deficiency is a common inherited condition
caused by a lack of a protease inhibitor (Pi) normally produced by the
liver. The role of A1AT is to protect cells from enzymes such as
neutrophil elastase. It classically causes emphysema (i.e. chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease) in patients who are young and non-
smokers.

receives IV fluids and oxygen, although does not require intubation.
Three days after his admission, he develops acute-onset shortness of
breath. The only past medical history reported was hay-fever as a child
and his mother has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. He smoked 1-
2 roll-up cigarettes per week and did not drink any alcohol.
His observations include a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute,
oxygen saturations of 91% on 12L of oxygen, a heart rate of 112 beats
per minute and blood pressure of 114/78 mmHg. His temperature was
36.9ºC. Examination revealed widespread crackles over both lung fields.
Chest x-ray reveals bilateral infiltrates.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). This
patient presents with the classical features of ARDS following a major
burn injury, which is a well-known precipitating factor. The diagnosis is
supported by the acute onset of respiratory symptoms, bilateral
infiltrates on chest x-ray, and hypoxaemia (requiring high-flow oxygen to
maintain saturations above 90%) occurring within a week of the initial
insult. The patient meets the Berlin criteria for ARDS, which includes
timing within 7 days of a known clinical insult, bilateral opacities not fully
explained by effusions or collapse, and respiratory failure not fully
explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia is incorrect because although this can
occur in burns patients due to immunosuppression, the bilateral nature
of the infiltrates and the timing (3 days) would be unusual. Hospital-
acquired pneumonia typically presents after 48 hours of admission with
unilateral changes initially, and often includes pyrexia and purulent
sputum, which are not present here.
Pneumonitis is incorrect as this term typically refers to inflammation of
lung tissue from non-infectious causes such as chemical injury or
autoimmune conditions. While smoke inhalation can cause chemical
pneumonitis, this would have been evident from admission rather than
developing after three days.
Renal failure is incorrect as while this can occur in burns patients due to
fluid loss and myoglobinuria, it would not explain the respiratory
symptoms and chest x-ray findings. Whilst pulmonary oedema can occur
in renal failure, the acute onset and bilateral infiltrates are more
consistent with ARDS.
Asthma attack is incorrect because despite the patient's history of atopy
(hay fever), the presentation is not consistent with acute asthma.
Asthma typically presents with wheeze rather than crackles, and the
chest x-ray would not show bilateral infiltrates. Additionally, asthma
would be unlikely to develop acutely in this setting without a clear
trigger.

Question 12 of 241
A 55-year-old HIV-positive American woman develops fever, cough and
fatigue after returning from her Thanksgiving holiday. Her chest
radiograph is normal. Her symptoms persist despite treatment with oral
co-amoxiclav. She undergoes a bronchoscopy and her bronchial
washings grow Histoplasma capsulatum.
What single treatment is most likely to resolve her symptoms?
explanation:
Histoplasma capsulatum is a rare fungus that can be found in the United
States of America that can cause respiratory symptoms in
immunocompromised patients. It should be treated with amphotericin or
itraconazole.
Caspofungin is also an antifungal drug, but it is more appropriate to treat
patients with Aspergillus infections.
Fluconazole is also an antifungal drug, but it is more appropriate to treat
patients with Candida infections.
Amphotericin or itraconazole are the pharmacological agents of
choice for histoplasmosis
Ivermectin is an anti-parasitic drug, but it is more appropriate to treat
other infections such as Strongyloides and Norwegian scabies.
Oral prednisolone is used to treat many respiratory diseases including
acute asthma. However, it is not appropriate for the initial treatment of a
fungal infection such as Histoplasma and appropriate anti-fungal
medication should be prescribed first.

Despite being tachypnoeic, this patient has a normal pCO2 which is a
sign of life-threatening asthma. This is despite therapy with
bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and magnesium. Therefore, this patient
needs referral to intensive care for intubation and ventilation.
BiPAP is not generally used in the treatment of asthma as there is
significant potential for air trapping so ventilation should be carried out
in intensive care. Therefore this option is incorrect.
To continue current management would not be an appropriate response
in this instance. This patient has failed to respond to therapy and is
showing signs of life-threatening asthma. Therefore, this patient needs a
referral to intensive care.
CPAP, similar to BiPAP, is not routinely used in the management of
asthma. CPAP does not help with ventilation and therefore CO2
clearance. It also poses a significant risk of air trapping in asthmatics.
Therefore, referral to intensive care would be more appropriate.
Although this patient has adequate saturations, it would be inappropriate
to wean oxygen as this does not address the normal pCO2 which is a
life-threatening sign.
Patients with features of acute life-threatening asthma who fail to
respond to treatment, should be referred to intensive care for
potential intubation and ventilation

Question 21 of 241
A 26 year old asthmatic woman is admitted to hospital following a
deliberate overdose of her usual theophylline tablets.
Which one of the following may be a complication of theophylline
toxicity?
explanation:
Theophylline is a methylxanthine derivative drug which is structurally
and clinically similar to caffeine. Aminophylline is the name given to
theophylline when it is ligand bound to the chemical ethylenediamine
which increases water solubility and hence aminophylline tends to be
the intravenous form. Methylxanthine derivatives are used clinically for
the treatment of bronchoconstriction in asthma, chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease and in neonatal apnoea. They work in a two-fold
fashion; firstly they inhibit the family of metabolic enzymes, the
phosphodiesterases which increase levels of cyclic adenosine
monophosphate and dampens the inflammatory cytokine cascade, and
secondly they are competitive antagonists at the endogenous adenosine
receptors located in the central nervous system, heart and lungs.
Theophylline poisoning presents with hypokalaemia,
hyperglycaemia, tachycardia and increased myocardial contractility
Inhibition of various phosphodiesterases causes a reduction in the
circulating population of inflammatory cytokines and also increases
cardiovascular and peripheral blood flow. Due to increased metabolism,
hypokalaemia is common and gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis is
stimulated causing a rise in the plasma glucose load.
Competitive antagonism at the adenosine receptor causes roughly the
opposite effects of adenosine. Whereas this drug is used clinically to
slow the heart rate and block transmission at the AV node, theophyllines
cause tachycardia and an increase in AV conduction, cardiac
automaticity and an increase in myocardial contractility, ultimately
leading to an increased cardiac output with hypertension and flushing.
Inhibition of adenosine receptors in bronchioles causes relaxation and
improved airflow, and in the central nervous system leads to agitation,
headache, anxiety, tremor and insomnia.
Other symptoms of methylxanthine toxicity include extreme nausea and
vomiting, pancreatitis, gastroesophageal irritation, psychiatric symptoms
and seizures. Tachyarrhythmias may deteriorate into ventricular rhythms
quickly which may be fatal. Competing metabolic acidosis and
respiratory alkalosis may cause a mixed arterial blood gas picture and
many electrolyte disturbances can occur but an unexplained
hyperglycaemia with a hypokalaemia is very suggestive of theophylline
toxicity. Theophylline has a narrow window of therapeutic efficacy and
patients may become toxic rapidly if drugs which inhibit their
metabolism are given concurrently, particularly antibiotics such as
macrolides or fluoroquinolones.
Management of theophylline toxicity is largely supportive with seizures
controlled by benzodiazepines or intubation. Phenytoin is best avoided
as it can worsen arrhythmia. Electrolyte abnormalities must be
corrected, particularly hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.
Hypertension and tachycardia may respond to beta-blockers but beware
of making the situation worse in an asthmatic patient. Verapamil is an
alternative. Ventricular rhythms should be electrically cardioverted.
Theophyllines are one of the few drugs which are highly adsorbed by
activated charcoal and this should be considered even beyond an hour
after ingestion due to the extended release nature of most preparations
and the drugs slowing of gastric emptying
Theophylline
Theophylline, like caffeine, is one of the naturally occurring
methylxanthines. The main use of theophyllines in clinical medicine is as
a bronchodilator in the management of asthma and COPD
The exact mechanism of action has yet to be discovered. One theory
suggests theophyllines may be a non-specific inhibitor of
phosphodiesterase resulting in an increase in cAMP. Other proposed
mechanisms include antagonism of adenosine and prostaglandin
inhibition

vomiting

What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Reposition the drain and increase the patient oxygen delivery
Leave the drain in situ and review in 24 hours
explanation:
Seeking a thoracic surgical opinion is correct as although the patient has
improved initially, it has now been 5 days since the chest drain was
When draining a pneumothorax, if after 3-5 days there is persistent
air leak (e.g. bubbling chest drain) or failure of the lung to re-
expand, a thoracic surgical opinion should be sought
inserted and there is still an ongoing persistent air leak with the chest
drain bubbling. Further management may now be required in the form of
pleurodesis or surgical resection etc.
Applying suction to chest drains is controversial and should not be used
unless under specialist guidance. The persistent air leak requires a
thoracic surgical opinion.
Removing the chest drain is incorrect as there is evidence of ongoing
persistent air leak and therefore non-resolution of the pulmonary
pathology.
Repositing of the drain is incorrect as there is no evidence that the drain
has moved or become displaced. Oxygen delivery can assist resolve a
pneumothorax however as it has been over 5 days further management
may be required.
The drain could be left in situ and review in 24 hours however it has
already been 5 days since it was originally inserted and there is evidence
of a persistent leak and therefore surgical opinion should be sought.

Sputum culture
Fungal spores seen - full speciation awaited
Based on the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management
option?
explanation:
The correct answer is itraconazole. This patient has a likely diagnosis of
histoplasmosis. This is based on the presence of retrosternal pain
alongside symptoms of a respiratory tract infection, combined with a
Amphotericin or itraconazole are the pharmacological agents of
choice for histoplasmosis
history of recent travel to the United States, where the causative
pathogen Histoplasma capsulatum is endemic, in parts. Further weight is
given to the diagnosis of histoplasmosis by the presence of fungal
spores in sputum culture. Of the options provided, only itraconazole is a
typical first-line treatment of histoplasmosis.
Co-trimoxazole is incorrect. This would be an appropriate initial
management option for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). This
would tend to appear in question stems as a cause for hypoxia with
exertional desaturation in immunosuppressed patients, rather than with
a productive cough and retrosternal pain. Diagnosis tends to be
confirmed on bronchoalveolar lavage rather than sputum culture.
Co-trimoxazole + prednisolone is incorrect as this would tend to be a
regime used for PJP with severe hypoxia rather than histoplasmosis.
Dapsone is incorrect, as this tends to be used as a second-line agent for
PJP if co-trimoxazole is ineffective or contraindicated, rather than
treatment for histoplasmosis.
Voriconazole is incorrect. Although from the same class of drugs as
itraconazole, voriconazole is more conventionally used for the treatment
of invasive aspergillosis, or its prevention, for example in allogeneic
stem cell transplant recipients. It is not typically used as a first-line
treatment option for histoplasmosis.

Question 24 of 241
A 56-year-old woman presents to clinic for review following
investigations and MDT discussion. She has chronic exertional
dyspnoea and following a restrictive pattern detected on spirometry and
changes on high-resolution CT scanning she has been diagnosed with
idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. What medication can be used to modify
disease progression?
explanation:
The correct answer is pirfenidone. Guidelines recommend supportive
care, pulmonary rehabilitation and supplementary oxygen, but in very
selective patients pirfenidone can be used. All of the other medication
options have been attempted, but are advised by NICE that there is
insufficient evidence to recommend their use. Patients are commonly
prescribed azathioprine and prednisolone but this does not affect the
disease course and does not help symptom control. Co-trimoxazole is
useful primarily in immunosuppression from HIV to prevent infection,
whilst sildenafil, a type 5 phosphodiesterase inhibitor, is more useful in
pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Question 34 of 241
A 52-year-old gentleman is admitted to hospital with a cough and fever.
He has been unwell for a week with high temperatures, coughing rusty
coloured sputum as well as small amounts of blood. He has no
significant past medical history but smokes ten cigarettes per day. A
chest X-ray shows right sided lower lobe consolidation with a pleural
effusion. An aspirate demonstrates low pH raising the suspicion of
empyema and a chest drain is requested under ultrasound guidance.
What factor may help predict drainage success or failure?
explanation:
The correct answer is septation density on ultrasound. This is a patient
with a possible empyema or parapneumonic effusion. The presence of
low pH in the effusion makes the former more likely. The presence of
septation density indicates various pockets within the effusion
indicating that even if a drain accesses any pocket in particular, it may
fail in draining all of the effusion. Protein level helps determine if an
effusion is a transudate or an exudate, whilst a low pH is most useful in
determining the risk of empyema. Consolidation may imply ongoing
pneumonia and may suggest a cause of the effusion.

history of weight loss and haemoptysis in a smoker raises concern for
an underlying malignancy. Infection is a possibility given his elevated
CRP and borderline pyrexia however the hypercalcemia makes
malignancy more likely. The most appropriate next test for this man is an
ultrasound-guided aspiration of the pleural fluid to both ascertain a
diagnosis and to alleviate his symptoms of dyspnoea. The pleural fluid
should be tested for biochemistry (including pH, protein, glucose and
LDH), microbiology and cytology.

aspiration will both add diagnostic value and alleviate his symptoms in
the first instance.

insufficient, then a bronchoscopy could be considered. A CT scan of the
chest would be required in advance of pursuing a bronchoscopy.

that helps to localise parathyroid adenomas. Although this man is
hypercalcemic, his parathyroid hormone levels are appropriately
suppressed thus there is no evidence of hyperparathyroidism.

reasonable test to perform however the concern based on the imaging
and clinical syndrome is of malignancy. Sputum MC&S is an essential
test when diagnosing respiratory infection but will not diagnose the
pleural effusion found on this man's chest radiograph.

© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The CT scan shows signet-rings and tram-tracks consistent with
bronchiectasis. This, in combination with normal pulmonary function
tests makes a diagnosis of emphysema less likely.
We can also exclude cystic fibrosis (CF). Some patients with CF now
survive to 45 years but it would be very unusual to reach this age without
significant respiratory problems in the past. An exam question would
never include such a bizarre history for CF.
There is also no evidence of situs inversus excluding Kartagener's
syndrome.
The bronchiectasis associated with lung cancer is confined to the area
distal to the tumour. It would therefore not explain the bilateral
symptoms.
The most likely diagnosis is therefore Bordetella pertussis infection, a
known cause of bronchiectasis.

higher rate of lung cancer than emphysema alone
This gentleman has a syndrome called combined pulmonary fibrosis and
emphysema (CPFE). Patients with CPFE have significantly higher rates
of lung cancer compared to those with emphysema (or idiopathic
pulmonary fibrosis) alone. They also have an increased risk of
developing pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is often less
responsive to medical treatments, meaning lung transplantation should
be considered in such cases.
CPFE is characterized by exertional dyspnoea, upper-lobe emphysema
and lower-lobe fibrosis, preserved lung volume and severely reduced
capacity of gas exchange. The preserved lung volumes are thought to
arise because of the counterbalanced effects of hyperinflation from
emphysema and the restrictive effects of pulmonary fibrosis. Both
mechanisms lead to reduced gas exchange, hence the significantly
reduced DLCO.
Option A - the correct answer
Options B - the HRCT findings of basal predominance fibrosis and
honeycombing is consistent with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)
pattern. Traction bronchiectasis may or may not be present in UIP. Non-
specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is radiologically characterized by
symmetric bilateral areas of ground-glass opacity with superimposed
fine reticular opacities but with no or only minimal honeycombing
Options C and D - as described above, patients with CPFE have a
significantly higher risk of developing lung cancer and/or pulmonary
arterial hypertension
Option E - Emphysema secondary to smoking is typically upper lobe
predominant, centrilobular and commonly manifests as small, localized
areas of low attenuation within the central portion of the secondary
pulmonary lobule on HRCT

Question 43 of 241
A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis after
presenting with an 18-month history of progressive dyspnoea. His latest
FVC is 60% of predicted. What is the average life expectancy for such a
patient from the time of diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer in this case is 3-4 years. Idiopathic pulmonary
fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive, irreversible lung disease characterized by
fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, leading to worsening dyspnoea and
reduced lung function. The prognosis for IPF varies widely, but on
average, the median survival from the time of diagnosis is around 3-4
years. In this patient with an FVC of 60% predicted, his life expectancy
would also fall within this range.
The option 3-6 months is incorrect because it represents a significantly
shorter life expectancy than what is typically seen in patients with IPF.
While some patients may have rapidly progressive disease or other
complicating factors that could lead to a shorter survival time, the
average life expectancy for someone with IPF is longer than this.
Similarly, the option 6-12 months is also incorrect as it underestimates
the average life expectancy for a patient with IPF. Although some
patients may have a more aggressive form of the disease or other
comorbidities that contribute to a worse prognosis, most patients can
expect to live longer than one year following their diagnosis.
The option 12-18 months still underestimates the typical life expectancy
for someone diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. While there
are cases where individuals may experience rapid progression of their
disease or have additional health issues that impact their prognosis, on
average, individuals diagnosed with IPF tend to live longer than 18
months.
Lastly, the option 8-12 years overestimates the average life expectancy
for someone with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Although there are
cases where individuals may survive beyond this timeframe due to
various factors such as early diagnosis and effective management
strategies, these cases are less common and do not represent the
average life expectancy for a patient with IPF.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

(CTPA) to exclude a pulmonary embolus (PE). The CTPA is reported as
finding no evidence of PE but notes a 7mm pulmonary nodule in the left
lower lobe.
How should the pulmonary nodule be investigated or monitored?
explanation:
The correct answer is CT chest in three months. This is a pulmonary
nodule which is larger than 5mm in size, and therefore has a significant
potential of growing. Based on this, the British Thoracic Society (BTS)
recommends surveillance. Only nodules which are greater than 8mm in
diameter and have a greater than 10% risk of malignancy, as assessed
by the Brock model (this can be accessed on the BTS website) should
undergo PET-CT and then, based on outcomes, be assessed for
obtaining a histological sample.
The timing of the follow-up CT is based on the nodule's size. A nodule of
5-6mm should be scanned at one year, whilst larger nodules should be
scanned at three months (unless being otherwise investigated).

Examination of the chest is normal with good air entry bilaterally and no

options: Peak expiratory flow rate measurements at both home and at work
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this case is occupational asthma, as
demonstrated by the timing of his breathlessness and wheeze as well as
the improvement in symptoms when on holiday. The diagnosis of
occupational asthma is best determined using peak expiratory flow rate
measurements taken at home and work to determine the difference in
the two - following this further investigation scan be performed to
determine the allergen causing the occupational asthma.

explanation:
This gentleman has Lofgren's syndrome a presentation of Sarcoidosis
characterised by Arthralgias, fevers, erythema nodosum and bilateral
hilar lymphadenopathy. It is typically more common in Scandinavian
patients and less common in Afro-Caribbean patients and typically has a
much better prognosis. This gentleman has stage 2 sarcoidosis as
indicated by the presence of BHL and pulmonary infiltrates on CXR. In
this case, oral corticosteroids are the preferred treatment. For less
symptomatic patients then supportive measures and NSAIDs for
arthralgia are the preferred treatment options. For patients who are not
responsive to steroids or steroid intolerant then immunosuppressant
agents such as methotrexate can be tried. RCHOP is a chemotherapy
regime used in lymphoma patients but the presence of non-caseating
granulomas should suggest a diagnosis other than lymphoma.
Lofgren's syndrome
Lofgren's syndrome is an acute form sarcoidosis characterised by
bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), erythema nodosum, fever and
polyarthralgia.
It typically occurs in young females and carries an excellent prognosis.

onset right-sided chest pain and mild shortness of breath. He is a
smoker with no previous medical history. His observations show heart
rate 92 beats/minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20

Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds on the right side. A
chest X-ray confirms a right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax
with approximately 3 cm rim of air laterally. You perform needle
aspiration, but after removing 1.5 litres of air, a repeat chest X-ray shows
the pneumothorax is still present with minimal improvement.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Attempt a second needle aspiration
Chest drain insertion
Conservative management with outpatient follow-up
Insertion of an ambulatory device
Referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS)
Question 53 of 241
A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden
onset right-sided chest pain and mild shortness of breath. He is a
smoker with no previous medical history. His observations show heart
rate 92 beats/minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20
breaths/minute, oxygen saturation 96% on air, and temperature 36.8°C.
Chest examination reveals reduced breath sounds on the right side. A
chest X-ray confirms a right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax
with approximately 3 cm rim of air laterally. You perform needle
aspiration, but after removing 1.5 litres of air, a repeat chest X-ray shows
the pneumothorax is still present with minimal improvement.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Chest drain insertion is the most appropriate next step in this case.
According to the British Thoracic Society (BTS) 2023 guidelines for the
management of spontaneous pneumothorax, if needle aspiration is
unsuccessful in resolving a pneumothorax, the next step should be chest
drain insertion. In this scenario, the patient has undergone needle
aspiration which has been unsuccessful, as evidenced by the repeat
A chest drain should be inserted if needle aspiration of a
pneumothorax is unsuccessful
chest X-ray showing minimal improvement despite removing 1.5 litres of
air. The patient is symptomatic with chest pain and mild shortness of
breath, and the pneumothorax is sizeable (3 cm rim of air laterally). A
chest drain will provide continuous drainage of the pleural space,
allowing the lung to re-expand. After insertion, the patient should be
monitored as an inpatient with daily reviews until the pneumothorax
resolves, at which point the drain can be removed and the patient
discharged with outpatient follow-up in 2-4 weeks.
Attempting a second needle aspiration is not recommended when the
first attempt has been unsuccessful. The BTS guidelines clearly indicate
that if needle aspiration fails to resolve the pneumothorax, progression
to chest drain insertion is warranted. Repeating the needle aspiration
would likely delay appropriate management and potentially subject the
patient to unnecessary discomfort and risk.
Conservative management with outpatient follow-up would be
appropriate for patients with a primary spontaneous pneumothorax who
have no or minimal symptoms, regardless of the size of the
pneumothorax. However, this patient is symptomatic with chest pain and
shortness of breath, and has already undergone an unsuccessful
intervention. Conservative management at this stage would be
inappropriate and potentially dangerous.
Insertion of an ambulatory device (such as a Rocket Pleural Vent) is an
alternative to needle aspiration or chest drain for symptomatic patients
without high-risk characteristics. However, in this case, needle aspiration
has already been attempted and failed, so progression to a chest drain is
the recommended approach according to the BTS algorithm.
Referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is typically
considered for patients with persistent air leak or insufficient lung re-
expansion despite chest drain insertion, or for those with recurrent
pneumothoraces. It is not the immediate next step after a failed needle
aspiration. VATS would be considered if the chest drain fails to resolve
the pneumothorax or if the patient experiences recurrent episodes.

A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with

alcoholic liver disease and has had previous admissions for
decompensated liver failure. She is not jaundiced or confused currently.
She has generalised abdominal tenderness, worse towards the
epigastrium. A chest X-ray demonstrates a right-sided pleural effusion. It
is aspirated and found to have a protein count of 37g/l. What is the most
likely cause of the effusion?
explanation:
The correct answer is pancreatitis. This is a patient with epigastric
abdominal pain and an exudative pleural effusion on a background of
heavy alcohol intake. Exudative effusions occur due to increased
leakiness of pleural capillaries. This can be due to infection,
inflammation or malignancy. Of the available options, this includes
pancreatitis and metastatic cancer. Transudates are caused by
increased venous pressure, occurring in cardiac failure, renal failure,
hepatic failure, as well as in Meig's syndrome, hypothyroidism and fluid
overload. Given the epigastric pain and alcohol history, pancreatitis is a
more likely cause than cancer and should be confirmed with serum and
fluid amylase.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (EAA, also known as hypersensitivity
pneumonitis) is a condition caused by hypersensitivity induced lung

largely caused by immune-complex mediated tissue damage (type III

thought to play a role in EAA, especially in the chronic phase.

but no focal neurological deficit. There are no respiratory symptoms or

Question 55 of 241
A 28-year-old man is trekking in the Himalayas and has reached an
altitude of 4,800 metres over several days. He develops a severe
headache, confusion, and difficulty walking. His companions report that
he has been increasingly unsteady on his feet for the past few hours. On
examination, he is disorientated to time and place, with marked ataxia
but no focal neurological deficit. There are no respiratory symptoms or
signs of pulmonary oedema. His oxygen saturation on room air is 78%.
Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation:
Descend and administer dexamethasone is correct because this patient
is displaying classical features of high altitude cerebral oedema (HACE):
rapid onset confusion, ataxia, severe headache, and hypoxia without
pulmonary findings. The mainstay of HACE management according to
UK guidelines is immediate descent combined with corticosteroids—
specifically dexamethasone—to reduce cerebral oedema. Descent
reverses hypobaric hypoxia rapidly, while dexamethasone mitigates
inflammation and blood-brain barrier permeability in HACE.
Management of high altitude cerebral edema (HACE) is with
descent + dexamethasone
Administer acetazolamide only would be inappropriate here as
acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness (AMS) or treats mild
AMS but does not address established HACE. It does not have sufficient
efficacy in reducing cerebral oedema acutely nor does it substitute for
descent or steroids in this context.
Administer nifedipine and oxygen would be more appropriate for high
altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE), where pulmonary vasoconstriction
leads to fluid accumulation in alveoli. This patient lacks any respiratory
symptoms or signs of pulmonary involvement; therefore, this approach
misses the primary pathology.
Administer dexamethasone only, while partially correct since steroids
are indicated for HACE, fails to address the underlying cause: ongoing
exposure to hypobaric hypoxia at high altitude. Without descent (or
simulated descent via hyperbaric chamber if available), symptoms will
likely worsen despite steroid therapy alone.
Descend and administer acetazolamide omits the key role of
corticosteroids in managing cerebral oedema specifically. While descent
helps reverse hypoxia—which is important—the addition of
acetazolamide offers little benefit once HACE has developed compared
to steroids like dexamethasone.
Altitude related disorders
There are three main types of altitude-related disorders: acute mountain
sickness (AMS), which may progress to high altitude pulmonary oedema
(HAPE) or high altitude cerebral oedema (HACE). All three conditions are
due to the chronic hypobaric hypoxia which develops at high altitudes
Acute mountain sickness is generally a self-limiting condition. Features
of AMS start to occur above 2,500 - 3,000m, developing gradually over 6-
12 hours and potentially last a number of days:

NICE guidelines says- 'Patients who have poor lung function but are
otherwise suitable for radical
radiotherapy should still be offered radiotherapy, provided the volume of
irradiated lung is small'.

those patients who are not suitable for surgery and with a peripheral
tumour(like the patient in the question), Stereotactic Ablative
Radiotherapy(SABR) given at a biologically equivalent dose of >100Gy is
the preferred treatment of choice.
A systematic review comparing outcomes of SABR and surgery in
patients with severe COPD revealed a higher 30-day mortality following
surgery but similar overall survival at 1 and 3 years.
NCCN(National Comprehensive Cancer Network) guidelines-2015 for
non-small cell lung cancer says SABR is an appropriate option for
patients with high surgical risk. SABR and sublobar resection both
achieve comparable cancer specific survival and primary tumour control.

lesions).
The central adipose deposition, 'moon face', new hypertension and
impaired glucose tolerance are all in keeping with Cushing's syndrome,
This is a paraneoplastic phenomenon seen in small cell lung cancer due

If these were metastatic deposits, the chest x-ray would show multiple

Mesothelioma is a cancer of the pleura due to asbestos exposure. There
is nothing in the vignette to suggest asbestos exposure. In questions
where asbestosis exposure may be relevant, the occupation of the
patient is usually that of a plumber or builder.
Adenocarcinoma of the lung is associated with gynaecomastia.
Squamous cell lung cancers can secrete parathyroid hormone-related
peptide which causes hypercalcaemia.

explanation:

(SIRS) as evidence by her tachycardia, tachypnoea and leucocytosis. The
most common cause, in this case, would be sepsis, however, history,
examination and investigations have not demonstrated a source. The
raised lactate suggests end organ hypo-perfusion. Routine biochemistry
demonstrates severe renal impairment which must be assumed to
represent stage 3 acute kidney injury (AKI) without previous values for
comparison. Arterial blood gas demonstrates a compensated metabolic
acidosis consistent with acute kidney injury, sepsis or SIRS.
With a negative septic screen we must consider alternative causes of
SIRS and in the context of stage 3 AKI and heavy blood and protein on
the urine dip, intrinsic renal pathology must be suspected.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (previously known as Wegener's
Granulomatosis) typically presents with non-specific symptoms, an
unwell patient and AKI with active urinary sediment. Nasal crusting due
to granulomas and a collapsed nasal septum may also be found. The
diagnosis is also suggestive by a positive cANCA with PR3 antibodies
although renal biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis.
Consider granulomatosis with polyangiitis when a patient presents
with ENT, respiratory and kidney involvement
