options: Take off mask to administer nebulisers
Give IV salbutamol instead of nebulised
Stop NIV whilst on 2 hourly nebulisers
explanation:
The correct answer is to take off the mask to administer nebulisers. This
is a patient with a severe exacerbation of COPD with type two respiratory
failure with acidosis not responding to medical therapy and needing NIV.
Whilst it is possible to give nebulisers into some NIV masks it is
preferable to administer nebulisers off NIV as a far greater proportion of
the drug reaches the airways, necessary for bronchodilation. Giving
nebulised medication into ongoing NIV is not recommended by the BTS
as the pressures reduce the effective dose reaching the airways.
Stopping nebulisers or NIV are both inappropriate as both are necessary.
'The Use of Non-Invasive Ventilation in the management of patients with
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease admitted to hospital with acute
type II respiratory failure. British Thoracic Society, October 2008'.
Acute exacerbation of COPD
Acute exacerbations of COPD are one of the most common reasons why
people present to hospital in developed countries.
The most common infective causes of COPD exacerbations are:
bacteria
Haemophilus influenzae (most common cause)
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Moraxella catarrhalis
respiratory viruses
account for around 30% of exacerbations
human rhinovirus is the most important pathogen
Features
increase in dyspnoea, cough, wheeze
there may be an increase in sputum suggestive of an infective
cause
patients may be hypoxic and in some cases have acute confusion
NICE guidelines from 2010 recommend the following:
increase the frequency of bronchodilator use and consider giving via
a nebuliser
give prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days

There are many contraindications to non invasive ventilation that must
be carefully considered. Patients must be awake and able to protect
their airway which this man although drowsy should be able to achieve
with a Glasgow Coma Score of 13. The patient is on maximal medical
therapy and there are few additional agents that would be helpful. His
ENT surgery is important but some years ago and there is no head or

is coughing up large volumes of sputum/secretions and this could pose
a compromise to his airway. It is difficult to understand if he has
capacity from the question but given his good premorbid function, active
treatment would likely be in his best interests.

use of non-invasive ventilation in acute respiratory failure. Following
these the Royal College of Physicians published guidelines in 2008.

This patient has granulomatosis with polyangiitis, with severe pulmonary
and renal involvement. He requires urgent immunosuppression. Of the
available options, the next best step is therefore to institute
cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone. The options may serve a

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, affecting both the upper and lower
respiratory tract as well as the kidneys.

The spirometry shows a restrictive picture consistent with pulmonary
fibrosis. The chest x-ray is also consistent with this diagnosis, showing
sub-pleural reticular opacities that increase from the apex to the bases
of the lungs.
Pirfenidone is currently the only drug recommended by NICE for the
treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

explanation:
Squamous cell lung cancer is the correct answer.
The patient's chest x-ray reveals a concerning mass in the left lung's hilar
region. Considering the patient's extensive history of smoking coupled
with respiratory symptoms, including haemoptysis, thrombocytosis, and
attributed to paraneoplastic secretion of parathyroid hormone-related
protein, is more commonly associated with squamous cell lung cancer.
Lung metastases is not correct. While the x-ray findings and symptoms
might suggest some form of lung disease, the patient's significant
smoking history combined with hypercalcemia lean more towards a
primary lung malignancy rather than metastatic disease.
Sarcoidosis is a viable differential diagnosis. The hypercalcemia and
thrombocytosis associated with sarcoidosis make it a potential
consideration. However, sarcoidosis typically presents with bilateral hilar
lymphadenopathy. The unilateral presentation in this case, combined
with the presence of haemoptysis, makes sarcoidosis less likely.
Small cell lung cancer is less likely. Although the patient's symptoms
could be consistent with small cell lung cancer, the presence of
hypercalcemia makes squamous cell lung cancer more likely.
Tuberculosis seems improbable in this case. While TB can indeed cause
haemoptysis, chronic cough, weight loss, and hilar lymphadenopathy on
imaging, other typical symptoms such as fever and night sweats are
absent. The combination of a hilar mass and thrombocytosis with the
patient's smoking history places lung cancer higher on the differential
list.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) refers to the prolonged domiciliary use
of oxygen for patients with medical conditions that result in a state of
chronic hypoxaemia (P 0  at or below 7.3kPa). The patient is assessed
so that the flow rate of oxygen they receive results in a waking oxygen
tension above 8kPa. LTOT is usually prescribed indefinitely and to be of
benefit has to be used for a minimum of 15 hours a day including at
night time.
The indications for LTOT are well established. The British Thoracic
Society (BTS) advises that LTOT may be of benefit in patients with the
following conditions:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Severe chronic asthma
Interstitial lung disease
Cystic fibrosis
Bronchiectasis
Pulmonary vascular disease
Primary pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary malignancy
Chronic heart failure
Patients with any of the above conditions can be assessed to see if they
would benefit from LTOT. BTS guidelines currently state that patients
should have a P 0  consistently at or below 7.3kPa on air at a time when
they are clinically stable (absence of exacerbation in previous five
weeks).
Another group of patients who can be prescribed LTOT are those with
chronic hypoxaemia and a P 0  between 7.3kPa and 8kPa and the
presence of either secondary polycythaemia or clinical and/or
echocardiographic evidence of pulmonary hypertension.
In the above case, the patient has chronic hypoxaemia. Ideally, this
patient would have his arterial blood gases analysed five weeks
following this exacerbation, but assuming that his results are similar and
his haemoglobin remains the same then he would require evidence of
pulmonary hypertension to benefit from LTOT thus an echocardiogram is
the best answer to this question.

A 57-year-old male presents with a three-month history of unintentional

He has just returned from a months holiday in India. He denies
haemoptysis or chest pain. He is a lifelong smoker. He has no past
medical history except a period of generalised limb weakness two years
ago when he was referred to outpatient neurology clinic and diagnosed
with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome following investigations. His
blood tests are unremarkable. However, his chest x-ray demonstrates a
rounded opacity in his right midzone, about 4 cm from his right main
bronchus.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient was treated four years ago for Lambert-Eaton syndrome
(LEMS), a neurological disorder characterised by limb weakness that
improves with exercise, affecting proximal muscles more than distal
muscle. It is caused by antibodies directed against voltage-gated
calcium channels and has a strong association with malignancy. Up to
half of all LEMS patients has an underlying malignancy, the most
common of which is small cell lung carcinoma. Neurological symptoms
often precede malignancy diagnosis by around 5 years.
1. O'Neill JH, Murray NM, Newsom-Davis J. The Lambert-Eaton
myasthenic syndrome. A review of 50 cases. Brain. 1988;111 ( Pt 3):577

explanation:
This gentleman is approaching the end of his life. He is on maximal
oxygen therapy and has expressed a wish not for escalation beyond
ward based care. His renal failure means that he is likely to accumulate
morphine and the most appropriate option for palliation of his
breathlessness is alfentanil - a short acting opiate.
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

peak of Mount Everest. He is keen to take a medicine to prevent against
acute mountain sickness. He has no past medical history and takes no

explanation:
If pharmacological prophylaxis of acute mountain sickness is required,
then acetazolamide is first line. This drug is a carbonic anhydrase
inhibitor which acts on the kidneys to generate a primary a metabolic
acidosis. A compensatory respiratory alkalosis occurs in response,
resulting in hyperventilation and improved oxygenation.
Dexamethasone, nifedipine and phosphodiesterase type V inhibitors
(e.g. sildenafil) can be used both in the treatment and prophylaxis of
acute mountain sickness, however for prophylaxis they are second line
agents.
Dorzolamide is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used in glaucoma.
Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) can be used to
prevent acute mountain sickness
Altitude related disorders
There are three main types of altitude-related disorders: acute mountain
sickness (AMS), which may progress to high altitude pulmonary oedema
(HAPE) or high altitude cerebral oedema (HACE). All three conditions are
due to the chronic hypobaric hypoxia which develops at high altitudes
Acute mountain sickness is generally a self-limiting condition. Features
of AMS start to occur above 2,500 - 3,000m, developing gradually over 6-
12 hours and potentially last a number of days:
headache
nausea
fatigue

explanation:
Bronchial carcinoid is a rare form of lung cancer but is much more
common in younger patients, typically presenting in late adolescence.
They are typically slow growing, well-differentiated tumours, explaining
the protracted history we see in this patient. The majority (approximately
75%) of bronchial carcinoid tumours arise in the proximal airways, hence
why symptoms include dyspnea, wheeze, cough, haemoptysis and/or
recurrent pneumonia. Patients may receive several courses of antibiotics
Bronchial carcinoid is the most common lung cancer in adolescents
and can present with recurrent pneumonia
to treat recurrent pneumonia before the tumour is diagnosed, as in this
case.
Studies have shown a positive association with smoking and the
development of bronchial carcinoid, but causality has not been proven
as with smoking and more common types of lung cancer.
Cavitation is rare. Pleural effusion is also uncommon but may be seen as
a complication of pneumonia caused by the obstruction from the
tumour. The chest x-ray description, in this case, is consistent with right
lower lobe collapse and a right pleural effusion.
Only 5-20 per cent of typical low-grade lung neuroendocrine tumours
(NETs) are associated with hilar or mediastinal adenopathy. Another clue
in this case to carcinoid is that contrast-enhanced CT scans frequently
show marked enhancement due to the vascular nature of the tumours.
Lung NETs tend to produce lower quantities of serotonin compared to
intestinal NETs, which explains why lung NETs have lower rates of
carcinoid syndrome, which is characterized by flushing, diarrhoea,
bronchospasm and can reflect metastases to the liver.
Option 1-4 - unlikely given the patient's age, relatively light smoking
history and absence of lymphadenopathy. Central carcinomas are more
likely to provide positive sputum cytology for malignant cells, whereas
that is not the case with central bronchial carcinoid due to an intact
bronchial mucosa usually overlying NETs.
Option 5 - the correct answer

explanation:
Nintedanib is a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor including the
receptors platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR) and ,
fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) 1-3, and VEGFR 1-3. It is
licensed for the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and is
endorsed by NICE guidelines when:
a) The person has a forced vital capacity (FVC) between 50% and 80% of
predicted
b) The company provides nintedanib with the discount agreed in the
patient access scheme and
c) Treatment is stopped if the disease progresses (a confirmed decline
in percent predicted FVC of 10% or more) in any 12month period.
Cyclophosphamide, rituximab and infliximab all have limited efficacy in
the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and are therefore not
recommended. Methotrexate is used primarily in the treatment of
rheumatoid arthritis and may itself cause pulmonary fibrosis.

Question 76 of 241
A 75-year-old retired electrician presents with a 3-month history of
progressive exertional dyspnoea, with associated chest pain. The chest
pain is right-sided and is not worse on deep inspiration. He also
describes intermittent haemoptysis and has noted 7kg of weight loss
since the chest pain started.
A CT scan of his thorax is carried out, the images for which are given
below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely cause of this imaging appearance?
explanation:
The CT shows concentric, nodular, pleural thickening. There also appears
to be interlobular fissure pleural involvement. Pleural thickening can be
due to a number of causes, one of which is mesothelioma. Other causes
include pleural metastases, pleural lymphoma, chronic inflammation
following empyema or recurrent pneumonia, and asbestos or silicosis-
related lung disease. Pleural thickening can be differentiated from the
appearance of a pleural effusion which is usually gravity dependent and
crescent shaped.
Mesothelioma is a cancer of the mesothelial layer of the pleural cavity
that is strongly associated with asbestos exposure, which may have
occurred due to this man's previous occupation as an electrician.
Small cell lung cancer is typically seen as a solid nodule within the lung,
often located centrally in the hilar or peri-hilar region. They readily
metastasise but do not generally involve the pleura.
Large cell lung carcinoma would usually manifest as a large peripheral
mass of solid attenuation and irregular margin. There is not usually
pleural involvement.
Sarcoidosis may show peri-lymphatic nodular thickening primarily
affecting the upper/mid zones, ground glass opacities, cysts, or
evidence of pulmonary fibrosis. It would not cause pleural thickening.
CT findings in pulmonary tuberculosis often show similar patterns of
disease as seen with chest x-rays, which would include fibronodular
opacities in upper lobes with or without cavitation. Tuberculosis can
involve the pleura but would present with a pleural effusion rather than
pleural thickening as seen here.

Question 77 of 241
A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a two-
week history of a dry cough, fever and retrosternal discomfort. He has a
past medical history of HIV and is poorly compliant with anti-retroviral
medications. He has recently returned from a holiday in Mississippi.
Observations:
Heart rate 95 beats per minute
Blood pressure 101/65 mmHg
Respiratory rate 24/minute
Spo2 93% on room air
Temperature 37.3C
The examination is unremarkable.
A chest x-ray demonstrates multifocal consolidation that extends to the
periphery of the lungs.
Sputum microscopy reveals yeasts.
What organism is most likely responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Mississippi and Ohio River valleys → ?histoplasmosis
Histoplasma capsulatum is the correct answer. The patient presents with
a dry cough, retrosternal discomfort, fever and chest x-ray evidence of
multifocal pneumonia after travelling from a region where
histoplasmosis is endemic. Yeasts identified on sputum microscopy are
also suggestive of a fungal rather than bacterial cause. Severe
histoplasmosis is more common in immunocompromised patients. His
history of poor compliance with HIV medications suggests he is at
further risk of developing severe fungal infections. Histoplasmosis is
often a self-limiting illness in an immunocompetent individual.
Coccidioides posadasii is incorrect. This causes coccidioidomycosis,
another endemic mycosis. While infection with this fungal organism can
cause respiratory failure and multifocal consolidation in patients with
HIV, it is not endemic to Mississippi. It is found in more arid regions
including southern California, southern Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico,
Utah and western Texas. it is also found in parts of South America and
Central America.
Legionella pneumophila is incorrect. This is a cause of a bacterial
atypical pneumonia. It is typically transmitted by inhaling contaminated
water droplets and so outbreaks have been linked to swimming pools
and air conditioning systems. It is not necessarily endemic to
Mississippi and sputum microscopy would not demonstrate a yeast,
which implies a fungal infection.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is incorrect. This is another potential cause of
pneumonia in a patient with HIV and probable low CD4 count. However,
yeasts would not be seen on sputum microscopy and this indicates a
fungal infection. Pseudomonas infections are also more common in
patients with pre-existing lung disease and indwelling vascular access.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is incorrect. This is one of the most common
causes of pneumonia. However, this typically causes lobar rather than
multifocal pneumonia. Additionally, the sputum sample may confirm that
organism rather than grow a yeast.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has mesothelioma, a type of malignancy of the
mesothelium, the tissue surrounding visceral organs including the lungs
and chest wall, heart and abdominal cavity. Most commonly the pleura
are affected. The biggest risk factor is asbestos exposure. With this
patient having worked as a builder, it is very possible that he has come
into contact with asbestos during his career. There is a visible
opacification on the left lateral chest wall of the chest x-ray, in keeping
with a pleural mass. Unlike other types of pulmonary malignancy that
commonly affect the bronchi and lung parenchyma, mesothelioma
affects the pleura and would therefore be located peripherally. One of the
most common and important symptoms to recognise is severe chest
wall pain as the tumour invades into the intercostal nerves.
Asbestosis is characterised by the development of lung fibrosis
secondary to asbestos exposure. Important distinguishing features
between asbestosis and mesothelioma are the presence of chest pain,
progressive shortness of breath and constitutional symptoms such as
fever, weight loss and night sweats. This patient is experiencing chest
pain, fatigue and shortness of breath. Furthermore, his full blood count
demonstrates microcytic anaemia which suggests the possibility of an
underlying malignancy.
A pleural effusion is a collection of fluid within the pleural space. An
exudative pleural effusion is more likely to become loculated.
Appearances of loculated pleural effusions can sometimes appear
similar to the chest x-ray shown in the question. However, the absence of
a raised white cell count, in combination with a significant history of
chest wall pain suggests an alternative diagnosis.
A pulmonary embolism is an important differential diagnosis given the
raised D-dimer and pleuritic-sounding chest pain. Occasionally, a
pulmonary embolism may have chest x-ray findings such as a wedge
infarction. However, a raised D-dimer can also indicate an underlying
malignancy. Furthermore, a peripherally-located lesion is unlikely to
represent a pulmonary embolism.
Small cell carcinoma is a pulmonary malignancy commonly associated
with tobacco use. As this patient has a history of COPD, it is likely that he
has a significant smoking history. Asbestos exposure and tobacco use
are synergistic to one another and increase the risk of malignancy. A
small cell carcinoma tends to be located more centrally on chest x-ray
films compared to mesothelioma as seen here.

symptomatic palliative treatments. However, while the disease burden
may be amenable to surgery, the patient's lung function testing may
restrict management options. Multiple studies have demonstrated FEV1

predicted for resective surgery1. Forced vital capacity is not
demonstrated to be a significant predictor of post-operative outcomes.

break. He has a past medical history of hypertension,
hypercholesterolaemia and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.
On examination, he has a heart rate of 101 beats/min with a blood
pressure of 140/98mmHg. His oxygen saturations are 90% on air with a
respiratory rate of 27 breaths/min. There is reduced air entry throughout
the right lung field.
A chest x-ray is requested, as shown below:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pulmonary metastases are relatively common but are not usually Mesothelioma
explanation:
This patient has evidence of pleural thickening along the borders of the
right lung which is most clear when making a comparison to the left lung
field. There is also an associated pleural effusion on the right side with a
visible fluid level that abuts the right costophrenic and costocardiac
angles. Overall, this significantly reduces the volume of the right lung.
This is most likely in keeping with a diagnosis of mesothelioma a rare
pleural malignancy that is largely associated with asbestos exposure.
The age of onset is typically between 60-85 years of age and presents
with dyspnoea, cough and chest pain. Chest x-ray findings of
mesothelioma include unilateral pleural thickening, reduced lung volume
size and lower zone interstitial fibrosis.
Congestive heart failure can present with pleural effusions. However,
more common chest x-ray findings include cardiomegaly, pulmonary
venous congestion and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. The unilateral
findings on this patient's chest x-ray are more suggestive of an
alternative diagnosis.
A parapneumonic effusion is a complication of viral or bacterial
pneumonia when fluid collects in the pleural space due to increased
permeability of the visceral pleura. Chest x-ray findings may be similar
with signs of pleural effusion and an overall reduced lung volume.
However, pleural thickening is not a feature of a parapneumonic
effusion.
A pulmonary embolism (PE) does not frequently give rise to chest x-ray
signs but can cause pleural effusions and Hampton hump sign (a
wedge-shaped opacification secondary to lung infarction). However, the
insidious onset of symptoms and pleural thickening make PE less likely.
symptomatic unless advanced. Rather, the patient will experience
constitutional symptoms and those of the primary malignancy. Chest x-
ray findings of pulmonary metastases usually include multiple round
nodules located in the peripheral lung fields. Unilateral pleural thickening
with an associated effusion is unlikely to present pulmonary
metastases.

A 35 year old chronic alcoholic male is admitted with severe epigastric

deterioriated over the next 2 days and he developed acute kidney injury
with severe respiratory distress to an extent needing mechanical
ventilation. Initial chest radiographs revealed widespread bilateral

options: Immediate initiation of glucocorticoid therapy to limit inflammatory progression
Placing patient in the prone position, allowing for greater recruitment of unaffected alveoli and improving PaO2/FiO2 ratio
Implementing a low tidal volume ventilation protocol
Changing from O2 to Nitric oxide at 5 ppm and titrating up until pt has an acceptable PaO2/FiO2 ratio
Aggressive diuresis to reduce pulmonary edema and vascular congestion
explanation:
Choice A - glucocorticoids to this point have not been shown to help
patients in the acute phase of ARDS. There is some evidence that they
may help in the fibroproliferative stage but not acutely
Choice B - While this is true, there is as of yet no good evidence showing
improved overall mortality.
Choice C - ARDS causes severe hypoxaemia, almost always requiring
invasive artificial ventilation. However, mechanical ventilation itself can
injure the damaged lungs causing ventilation-induced lung injury. The
main goal of treatment is to minimise any additional damage while
maintaining adequate gas exchange. This has been effectively done by
maintaining low tidal volume ventilation. A Cochrane Database review
(1) and meta-analysis (2) suggest that a strategy of low tidal volume
ventilation reduces the absolute mortality by about 7-9% as compared to
using higher tidal volumes. This converts to a Number needed to treat
(NNT) of between 11-15 people with ARDS to prevent one death by using
low tidal volume ventilation.
Choice D - Nitric oxide does improve PaO2/FiO2 ratio but has not shown
improved survival
Choice E - Since the infiltrate of ARDS is primarily inflammatory, diuretics
are not particularly effective. Overdiuresis also runs the risk of
hemodynamic compromise, further decreasing the patient's already
insufficient oxygen delivery to tissues.

volumes in adults for acute lung injury and acute respiratory
distress syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2004;

has worked as an electrician 20 years ago and believes that he may have

options: Normal ratio of FEV1 to FVC and normal FEV1
FEV1 to FVC ratio <0.7 but improves with inhaled steroids
FEV1 to FVC ratio <0.7 but improves with inhaled salbutamol
explanation:
The correct answer is FEV1 to FVC ratio >0.7, which would be in keeping
with a restrictive pattern if the FEV1 compared to expected was also
reduced. In asbestosis, there is restriction of lung expansion due to
pleural disease, limiting expansion of lung volume as the plaques are not
as expansile as pulmonary tissue. This stops the lungs from fully
expanding leading to a restrictive picture on spirometry. Obstructive
patterns, with a decreased ratio of FEV1 to FVC would be associated
with COPD and asthma.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is basal atelectasis - a
condition where mucous trapped in the bronchial tree results in small
airway obstruction. There is often segmental lung collapse due to the
basal atelectasis. Management is with chest physiotherapy and saline
nebulisers to encourage production of the mucous.

A 26-year-old man is reviewed in the asthma clinic. Despite therapy with
high dose fluticasone / salmeterol montelukast and oral theophylline, he
has suffered a 4th exacerbation in the past year and is now unable to
reduce his dose of oral prednisone below 10mg without a significant
increase in shortness of breath and wheeze. On examination his blood
pressure is 123/80 mmHg, his pulse is 80 beats per minute and regular.
Auscultation of the chest reveals quiet wheeze. His peak flow is 429
ml/min, (550 predicted). Eosinophils are elevated at 3.9 x 10(9)/l. IgE is
within the normal range.
Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Mepolizumab is an anti-IL5 monoclonal antibody and represents the
optimal intervention here. It binds to IL5 and prevents it from binding to
its receptor. IL5 is a cytokine which promotes growth in eosinophil
numbers and activity. By blocking IL5 mepolizumab down-regulates
eosinophil activity and has been shown to significantly improve
symptoms in resistant asthma. Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal
antibody, it is effective in treating resistant asthma with evidence of
raised IgE and allergic symptoms and is often considered for similar
Mepolizumab may be used for asthma with high eosinophils
patients to those treated with mepolizumab, although eosinophil count
and IgE drive which of the two therapies are used.
Mycophenolate is not utilised as a disease modifying agent in resistant
asthma, but is primarily used for the treatment of lupus nephritis and as
an anti-rejection agent. Infliximab is an anti-TNF monoclonal antibody
used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease and arthritides.
Tiotropium is primarily used in the treatment of COPD, and is less
effective than other options listed in the treatment of resistant asthma.
Nebulisers only have a role in treating asthma where patients are unable
to administer beta agonist therapy using a conventional inhaler and
spacer device.

Looking back at his notes you note that significant (> 20%) diurnal
variation has been noted in his peak flows.
The patient is currently prescribed a short-acting beta-2 agonist along
with a combination inhaler containing a long-acting beta-2 agonist and
corticosteroid.
What is the most appropriate additional medication?
explanation:
The correct answer in this case is inhaled tiotropium. Tiotropium is a
long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) that is commonly used as an
additional bronchodilator in the management of COPD. According to the
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines,
adding a LAMA such as tiotropium is recommended when patients with
COPD continue to experience breathlessness or exacerbations despite
treatment with a long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) and inhaled
corticosteroid (ICS).
Oral modified-release aminophylline is not the most appropriate choice
because it is a methylxanthine bronchodilator that has a narrow
therapeutic index and requires regular monitoring of serum levels. It is
generally reserved for cases where other treatments have failed or are
contraindicated.
Short-acting muscarinic agonist would be an incorrect choice because
these medications are not used in the treatment of COPD. In fact, short-
acting muscarinic antagonists (SAMA), such as ipratropium, may be
used as bronchodilators in COPD but are not the most appropriate
option here given that the patient already has LABA/ICS therapy and
adding a LAMA like tiotropium would provide better symptom control.
Oral prednisolone would not be the best option in this scenario, as it is
typically used for acute exacerbations of COPD rather than as part of
routine maintenance therapy. Long-term oral corticosteroid use has
significant side effects and should be avoided unless absolutely
necessary.
Finally, oral roflumilast could be considered for patients with severe
COPD who have chronic bronchitis symptoms and frequent
exacerbations, but it is not the first choice for managing persistent
breathlessness in this patient. Adding a LAMA like tiotropium would be
more appropriate according to the NICE guidelines.
In summary, the most appropriate additional medication for this patient
COPD - still breathless despite using SABA/SAMA and a LABA + ICS
→ add a LAMA
with COPD and persistent breathlessness despite LABA/ICS therapy is
inhaled tiotropium.

The diagnosis here is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). It
is a hypersensitivity reaction to the fungus Aspergillus causing an
eosinophilic pneumonia. Presenting symptoms are similar to asthma
and include dyspnoea, dry cough and wheeze. Patients with ABPA are
commonly misdiagnosed as having asthma and standard treatments for
asthma (e.g. salbutamol inhalers) have little benefit. This patient
describes similar symptoms of shortness of breath and a dry cough.
Furthermore, her blood tests demonstrate a raised eosinophil count and
IgE level, both of which point towards ABPA. The treatment of choice is
oral prednisolone to help facilitate the clearing of pulmonary infiltrates.
Intravenous amphotericin B is used in the treatment of systemic fungal
infections, including invasive Candida albicans or invasive aspergillosis.
Invasive aspergillosis is uncommon and is mostly seen in
immunosuppressed patients and presents with systemic illness.
Amphotericin B is not routinely given first-line to treat infections with
Aspergillus. Instead, fluconazole or itraconazole can be given, if
indicated. However, the combination of wheeze, shortness of breath, and
dry cough are more in keeping with ABPA, for which oral corticosteroids
are the most appropriate treatment.
Intravenous co-trimoxazole and methylprednisolone are used in the
treatment of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PCP). PCP presents in a
similar way to this patient with dyspnoea, fever and a dry cough.
However, PCP is mostly seen in immunocompromised patients, such as
those with HIV or on immunosuppressant medications. There is nothing
in this patient's history to suggest immunosuppression, therefore it is
likely that PCP is not the underlying diagnosis.

poorly controlled asthma, for which oral corticosteroids is the preferred
method of treatment.
Salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers are used in the acute treatment
of asthma. However, it plays no role in the treatment of ABPA.
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis results from an allergy to
Aspergillus spores. In the exam questions often give a history of
bronchiectasis and eosinophilia.

A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 2-day
history of haemoptysis. In the past 3-4 weeks he also reports worsening
shortness of breath with mild central chest pain. His past medical
history includes hypertension for which he takes amlodipine 5mg daily.
On examination, his saturations are 90% on air. His heart rate is 72/min
and regular with a blood pressure of 115/85mmHg. There is reduced air
entry at the right base. During the examination, he coughs up
approximately 100mls of fresh blood.
Imaging of his chest is requested, as shown below.
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient's chest x-ray and CT scan show multiple small nodules
throughout the lung fields. Additionally, on the CT scan, there are a few
well-defined regions of airspace opacification (as demonstrated by the
grey-coloured, round lung markings) which can represent consolidation
or pulmonary haemorrhage. In keeping with the history of haemoptysis
and shortness of breath, pulmonary haemorrhage is a likely cause of this
finding. Further inspection of the chest x-ray shows blunting of the right
costophrenic angle demonstrating a likely pleural effusion.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a type of small vessel
vasculitis that is responsible for causing respiratory symptoms such as
sinusitis, nasal crusting, shortness of breath and pulmonary
haemorrhage. The disease can also cause multiple nodules (with or
without cavitation) to arise in the lung parenchyma similarly to that seen
in this patient. Pleural effusions are seen in up to 20% of chest x-rays of
GPA patients. The disease can initially manifest around middle-age.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis also causes respiratory
symptoms. Pulmonary nodules and pleural effusions may also be seen
on imaging, however, pulmonary haemorrhage is not a typical symptom.
Instead, wheeze and sinusitis tend to feature.
Pulmonary emboli are capable of causing shortness of breath, hypoxia
and haemoptysis (as seen in this patient). They are diagnosed using a
CT pulmonary angiogram to assess for filling defects in the pulmonary
arteries. Normally, chest x-ray appearances are completely normal.
However, in some cases (and also on CT imaging), there is evidence of
pulmonary infarction. Pulmonary infarctions create wedge-shaped
opacifications without the presence of air bronchograms. Instead, this
patient's imaging shows multiple lung nodules, pleural effusion and
airspace opacification suggestive of pulmonary haemorrhage.
Rheumatoid arthritis has multiple respiratory features including lower
zone fibrosis, pulmonary nodules, pleural effusions and bronchiolitis
obliterans. However, rheumatoid arthritis does not cause haemoptysis,
making it the incorrect answer.
Sarcoidosis causes a range of pulmonary features from hilar
lymphadenopathy to diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and fibrosis. The
disease is most common in young Afro-Caribbean women and although
shortness of breath and a dry cough are common symptoms,
haemoptysis is not seen.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is now the preferred term for Wegener's
granulomatosis. It is an autoimmune condition associated with a
necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, affecting both the upper and lower
respiratory tract as well as the kidneys.

respiratory tract, and vasculitis of small-to-medium-sized vessels. The
presence of a pulmonary haemorrhage and renal failure, combined with
a strongly positive ANCA makes this the most likely diagnosis.
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is incorrect. Although
the patient has a positive aspergillus-specific antibody result and raised
total serum IgE, the clinical features, in this case, do not support a
diagnosis of ABPA. ABPA presents with shortness of breath, cough, and
wheezing. As Aspergillus fumigatus spores are common in the
environment and almost everyone is exposed to them, low levels of
antibodies to A. fumigatus are found in many patients and are often not
clinically significant.
Churg-Strauss syndrome is incorrect. Churg-Strauss syndrome, also
known as allergic granulomatous angiitis, is a rare disease characterised
by the triad of asthma, pulmonary infiltrates, and hypereosinophilia.
Although this remains within the differential diagnosis, the acute onset,
presence of renal failure, and strongly positive ANCA with a PR3 subtype
favours the diagnosis of Wegener's granulomatosis. Churg-Strauss
syndrome is classically associated with the MPO subtype of ANCA.

with ENT, respiratory and kidney involvement
Goodpasture's disease is incorrect. Pulmonary haemorrhage and renal
failure are classical features of this condition. However, this condition is
associated with anti-GBM antibodies rather than ANCA, making this a
less likely diagnosis.
Hypereosinophilic syndrome is incorrect. Hypereosinophilic syndrome
(HES) is a diagnosis of exclusion and should be made only after reactive
and clonal eosinophilia have been excluded. The absence of eosinophilia
makes this a less likely diagnosis.

A 22-year-old man presents to rheumatology clinic with chronic lower
back pain and early morning stiffness. He has past medical history of
asthma and is on regular steroid inhalers and suffers from multiple
exacerbations annually. He is due to see a respiratory physician to help
better manage his symptoms. Clinical examination shows demonstrate
Schober's sign. Pelvic X-rays demonstrate sacroiliitis. A diagnosis of
ankylosing spondylitis is made. The patient is concerned about using
NSAIDs to control his symptoms; what factor may suggest that NSAID-
sensitive asthma?
explanation:
The correct answer is nasal polyps. Asthmatics are typically taught to be
aware that NSAID's can worsen asthma but not all patients are sensitive.
The presence of nasal polyps is associated with a higher chance of
reaction to NSAID's, whilst having had NSAID's and suffered no reaction
within the last 12 months reduces the chance of further reactions. The
other options do not predict a reaction ITU admissions and high
frequency of admissions can suggest poorly managed or brittle asthma.
Source:
'Drug allergy: diagnosis and management' Clinical Guideline [CG183].
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, Sep. 2014.

The PaCO2 level which is at the upper limit of normal is very worrying

may be of benefit, the description that she is anxious and possibly
disoriented are concerning features and may indicate that shes tiring. In
light of this getting a timely review by an anaesthetist/intensivist is of
the utmost importance and should be the next immediate step. Giving
hydrocortisone intravenously is unlikely to be of any benefit and
considering antibiotics is not a priority in this situation where time is of
the essence. Hence waiting another 10 minutes to do another arterial
blood gas with to preceding action may potentially be fatal.

very loudly and occasionally stops breathing at night. He also falls
asleep easily during the day while watching television or reading. He had
bilateral tonsillectomies and adenoidectomy as a child. On examination,
his height is 1.80m and his weight is 100kg. He has lost 15kg of weight
in the last six months but his symptoms have persisted. His GP refers
him for a sleep study which is suggestive of moderate sleep apnoea.
What initial management option should be recommended?
Further weight loss and repeat sleep study thereafter
Lifestyle advice including sleep hygiene
Mandibular advancement splint
Referral for CPAP

very loudly and occasionally stops breathing at night. He also falls

his height is 1.80m and his weight is 100kg. He has lost 15kg of weight
in the last six months but his symptoms have persisted. His GP refers
him for a sleep study which is suggestive of moderate sleep apnoea.
What initial management option should be recommended?
options: Further weight loss and repeat sleep study thereafter
explanation:
Patients with symptoms suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
that affect their quality of life should be offered continuous positive
airway pressure (CPAP) if they have moderate or severe OSA, in addition
to lifestyle advice.
Weight loss as part of lifestyle advice may be appropriate as first-line
treatment for patients with mild sleep apnoea. However, this patient has
already tried to lose weight without any benefit. Furthermore, they have
moderate sleep apnoea and should be offered CPAP alongside lifestyle
Following weight loss, CPAP is the first-line treatment for
moderate/severe obstructive sleep apnoea
advice. Patients who feel that their OSA has resolved following lifestyle
modification can have a trial of stopping treatment for two weeks and
then an evaluation of their symptoms or a repeat sleep study.
Lifestyle advice regarding sleep hygiene, reducing alcohol and smoking
and weight loss is important but NICE recommends that it should be
provided alongside CPAP in patients with moderate to severe OSA.
A mandibular advancement splint is not first-line in treating sleep
apnoea but can be offered to those who do not tolerate CPAP and have
good dental health. This patient should thus be offered CPAP first.
CPAP is first-line for sleep apnoea, but referral to ENT may be
appropriate if he is unable to tolerate CPAP or other interventions first.
An ENT physician may recommend tonsillectomy or other oropharyngeal
surgery.

This lady with a history of asthma and sinusitis has presented
systemically unwell with diarrhoea, a right common peroneal nerve palsy,
vasculitic rash and has evidence of a nephritis. Investigations show a
significant eosinophilia and immunological screen has shown she is P-
ANCA positive. The most likely diagnosis is, therefore, Churg-Strauss
syndrome. This is a small vessel vasculitis with eosinophilic infiltration
and granulomatous formation that is characterised by chronic sinusitis,
asthma and eosinophilia. Systemic features of malaise, myalgia, fever
and weight loss are common. Other symptoms and signs depend on
other organ systems involved which most commonly are the lung
(asthma, pneumonitis) and skin (purpura, subcutaneous nodules);
however, any organ system can be affected including the cardiovascular
(heart failure, myocarditis), gastrointestinal (gastroenteritis, ischaemia,
bleeding), renal (glomerulonephritis, hypertension), and central nervous
systems (mononeuritis multiplex). ANCA is positive in approximately
60% of cases and is predominantly P-ANCA.
Infective endocarditis could account for some of her symptoms however
the absence of a heart murmur and the multisystem involvement, in this
case, makes it less likely. Wegener's granulomatosis is another
granulomatous small vessel vasculitis which most commonly presents
with lesions in the upper respiratory tract (rhinorrhoea, sinusitis, saddle
nose deformity), lungs (infiltrates and pulmonary haemorrhage) and
kidneys (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis). It is classically C-ANCA
positive. The history of immunological screen of this case is, therefore,
more typical of Churg-Strauss syndrome. E.coli gastroenteritis would be
unlikely to present in this fashion.
Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that classically
presents with abdominal pain, weight loss and change in bowel habit.
There are often extra-intestinal manifestations involving the mouth, skin,
eyes, joints and episodes of perianal abscess or anal fissure. Crohn's
disease could account for some of this lady's symptoms but again is
less likely than Churg-Strauss syndrome.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
(Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is now the
preferred term for Churg-Strauss syndrome. It is an ANCA associated
small-medium vessel vasculitis.

always have some smoking history. Furthermore, he has no lung or liver

are obese often have lots of soft tissue in the neck that occlude the
airway when asleep and the tone falls. Therefore, the carbon dioxide

Question 106 of 140
A 67-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden
onset left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. He has a 40-pack-
year smoking history and was diagnosed with COPD three years ago. On
examination, he is tachypnoeic but haemodynamically stable; oxygen
saturations are 93% on room air. A chest X-ray confirms a moderate left-
sided pneumothorax that appears accessible for intervention.
What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
explanation:
Chest drain insertion is the correct answer because this patient has both
symptomatic pneumothorax and high-risk features: age over 50 with
significant smoking history, underlying lung disease (COPD), and hypoxia
(saturations below normal). According to the 2023 BTS guidelines,
symptomatic patients with high-risk characteristics require chest drain
insertion if it is safe to do so. This approach reduces morbidity and risk
of deterioration compared to less invasive measures in such patients.
Conservative care as an outpatient would be inappropriate here due to
the presence of symptoms and multiple high-risk features. Conservative
Symptomatic pneumothorax patients with high-risk features (e.g.
underlying lung disease) require a chest drain
management is reserved for patients who are minimally symptomatic
and have no high-risk factors, which does not apply in this case.
Ambulatory device insertion may be considered in selected cases of
primary spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk features or
significant symptoms. However, ambulatory devices are not
recommended by BTS guidelines for secondary pneumothoraces or
those with significant comorbidity, hypoxia, or older age with a heavy
smoking history.
Needle aspiration can be used as first-line management in some cases
of primary spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk criteria. In
symptomatic patients with secondary causes or other risk factors like
this man, needle aspiration alone is unlikely to be effective or safe;
current guidance recommends proceeding directly to chest drain
insertion.
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is indicated in cases of
persistent air leak, failure of lung reexpansion despite chest drain, or
recurrent episodes—not as initial management of a first episode where a
chest drain is indicated according to current UK practice.

pneumonia. He has been intubated and ventilated for 24 hours due to
worsening hypoxaemia. Despite being on 80% inspired oxygen (FiO2)
and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 12 cmH2O, his
oxygenation remains poor. His chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates
consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

Which intervention is most likely to improve this patient's oxygenation?
explanation:
Prone positioning for 16 hours is the most appropriate intervention for
this patient with moderate-to-severe ARDS. The patient has a PaO2/FiO2
ratio of approximately 10.1 kPa (8.1/0.8), which is consistent with severe
Prone positioning is helpful in ventilated patients with ARDS
ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 < 13.3 kPa or 100 mmHg). Prone positioning has been
shown to significantly improve oxygenation and reduce mortality in
patients with severe ARDS. The PROSEVA trial demonstrated that early
application of prolonged prone positioning sessions (at least 16 hours
per day) in patients with severe ARDS resulted in significantly decreased
28-day and 90-day mortality compared with supine positioning. Prone
positioning works by improving ventilation-perfusion matching, reducing
ventral-dorsal transpulmonary pressure gradient, and promoting more
homogeneous ventilation. It also helps in the drainage of secretions and
reduces the compression of lung tissue by the heart and mediastinal
structures.
Increase FiO2 to 100% is not the best option for this patient. While
increasing FiO2 may temporarily improve oxygenation, the patient is
already on a high FiO2 (80%), and further increases expose the patient to
oxygen toxicity without addressing the underlying pathophysiology of
ARDS. Prolonged exposure to high oxygen concentrations can lead to
absorption atelectasis and oxidative damage to the lungs, potentially
worsening lung injury. The focus should be on interventions that improve
lung recruitment and ventilation-perfusion matching, rather than simply
increasing oxygen delivery.
Administration of inhaled nitric oxide may transiently improve
oxygenation in some patients with ARDS by selectively dilating
pulmonary vessels in ventilated areas of the lung, thereby improving
ventilation-perfusion matching. However, multiple randomised controlled
trials have failed to demonstrate a mortality benefit with its use in ARDS.
Additionally, it is associated with significant costs, potential for
methaemoglobinaemia, and rebound hypoxaemia upon discontinuation.
Current guidelines do not recommend the routine use of inhaled nitric
oxide in ARDS.
Neuromuscular blockade for 48 hours can improve patient-ventilator
synchrony and may be beneficial in early, severe ARDS. The ACURASYS
trial showed improved outcomes with 48 hours of cisatracurium in
patients with severe ARDS. However, a more recent and larger trial
(ROSE) did not confirm these benefits. While neuromuscular blockade
might be considered in this patient, prone positioning has stronger
evidence supporting its use in improving outcomes in severe ARDS and
would be the preferred initial intervention.
High-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) was once thought to be
beneficial in ARDS by providing small tidal volumes and maintaining
alveolar recruitment. However, two large randomised controlled trials
(OSCAR and OSCILLATE) demonstrated no benefit or even harm with
HFOV compared to conventional lung-protective ventilation strategies in
adults with ARDS. Current evidence does not support the routine use of
HFOV in adult ARDS patients, and it may even increase mortality in some
cases.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is caused by the increased
permeability of alveolar capillaries leading to fluid accumulation in the
alveoli, i.e. non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It is a serious condition
that has a mortality of around 40% and is associated with significant
morbidity in those who survive.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF, previously termed cryptogenic
fibrosing alveolitis) is a chronic lung condition characterised by
progressive fibrosis of the interstitium of the lungs. Whilst there are
many causes of lung fibrosis (e.g. medications, connective tissue
disease, asbestos) the term IPF is reserved when no underlying cause
exists.
IPF is typically seen in patients aged 50-70 years and is twice as
common in men.

in prevalence within the non-HIV population. There are over 100 different

environmental nature of the organisms.

pulmonary non-tuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) infection in
immunocompetent individuals. NTM infection in the non-HIV population

explanation:
Klebsiella pneumonia is particularly associated with diabetic and
alcoholic patients. It leads to a cavitating upper lobe pneumonia.
Differentials for this lady would include lung cancer and tuberculosis but
these would usually be associated with weight loss and travel to eastern
Europe or Asia respectively.
Klebsiella most commonly causes a cavitating pneumonia in the
upper lobes, mainly in diabetics and alcoholics

A 35-year-old man presents with a chronic productive cough which has
been affecting him for several years. He has no other past medical
history apart from recurrent otitis media as a child. He takes no regular
medications. He has never smoked and has no history of passive
smoking and works as a solicitor. He has no pets at home and has no
mould that he is aware of. On examination there is finger clubbing, he
appears underweight, there are coarse late-inspiratory crepitations and a
mild wheeze. Also, his heart sounds are louder on the right side, and his
apex beat is also only present on the right. What further investigation
would most likely confirm the diagnosis?
Immunological testing for Aspergillus fumigatus specific IgE
CFTR gene testing
Sputum MCS
Sputum Zeil-Neilsen staining and microscopy.
Ciliary function tests
Question 117 of 140
A 35-year-old man presents with a chronic productive cough which has
been affecting him for several years. He has no other past medical
history apart from recurrent otitis media as a child. He takes no regular
medications. He has never smoked and has no history of passive
smoking and works as a solicitor. He has no pets at home and has no
mould that he is aware of. On examination there is finger clubbing, he
appears underweight, there are coarse late-inspiratory crepitations and a
mild wheeze. Also, his heart sounds are louder on the right side, and his
apex beat is also only present on the right. What further investigation
would most likely confirm the diagnosis?
options: Immunological testing for Aspergillus fumigatus specific IgE
explanation:
The correct answer is ciliary function tests. This would confirm a
diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia. Ciliary function is commonly
tested by the use of saccharin. Saccharin is placed 1cm behind the
inferior turbinate and the test is positive if the patient does not taste
sweetness within 20min. This is because if cilia work normally they will
sweep the sweet saccharin inwards, allowing the patient to taste it.
Cilia line the upper respiratory tract, including the eustachian tubes, and
moves normally in a coordinated fashion to help clear mucous,
secretions and debris. In ciliary dyskinesis there is less movement or it is
less coordinated. For this patient there is first a clear history and signs
of bronchiectasis with chronic productive cough, bilateral late inspiratory
crepitations and clubbing. But the history of otitis media, young patient
and indications dextrocardia are all suggestive of primary ciliary
dyskinesis. Cystic fibrosis is less likely due to the absence of
gastrointestinal symptoms and signs, there is no travel history,
heamoptysis or other factors to suggest TB, and there is no history of
asthma making fungal infection and immunological response unlikely.

explanation:
This patient most likely has obesity hypoventilation syndrome as
characterised by his raised carbon dioxide levels in the morning, as
opposed to the evening.

on auscultation but she has an early diastolic murmur. She has already

ECG
Renal function blood tests
Echocardiogram
High-resolution CT chest
Right heart catheterisation
Question 119 of 140
A 52-year-old woman presents with worsening exercise tolerance. Her
GP has recently increased her asthma treatment but this has not helped,
nor does she have any relief from her salbutamol inhaler. She has no
other known medical history. On examination, her lung fields sound clear
on auscultation but she has an early diastolic murmur. She has already
had a chest X-ray demonstrating enlarged proximal pulmonary arteries.
Which investigation is most likely to provide the correct diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is right heart catheterisation to diagnose pulmonary
arterial hypertension. The history is primarily of worsening shortness of
breath in a middle-aged person with clear lung fields and a diastolic
murmur. The chest X-ray with enlarged proximal pulmonary arteries is
highly suggestive. Whilst an ECG or echocardiogram may show features
of pulmonary arterial hypertension right heart catheterisation is the gold
standard and would be most diagnostic.

for her asthma review.
Unfortunately, she has been admitted to hospital three times in the last
year with asthma exacerbations, requiring 2-3 days in hospital but never
requiring intubation or intensive care admission. This is on a background
of multiple admissions to hospitals in previous years.
On review, she reports wheeze associated with dyspnoea on most days
and this is usually triggered by exertion. There is a non-productive cough
most mornings which settles throughout the course of the day. There is

oxygen saturation 98% on room air, heart rate 80/min regular, blood

clubbing, cervical lymphadenopathy or elevation of the jugular venous

explanation:
This patient has inadequately controlled asthma as evidenced by the
three admissions to hospital and ongoing cough, wheeze and dyspnoea.
There is a serum eosinophilia and elevated fraction of exhaled nitric
oxide (FENO), both suggesting eosinophilic inflammation as an
important driver of this patient's asthma. Such patients are eligible for
anti-interleukin-5 therapy such as mepolizumab.
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously has
been shown to significantly reduce asthma exacerbations and is
particularly useful in patients on long-term steroid therapy.
There are several inflammatory phenotypes in asthma most commonly
described as eosinophilic, neutrophilic, mixed, and paucigranulocytic.
Mepolizumab and other anti-IL-5 therapies can be used in adults
with eosinophilic asthma
The presence of eosinophilic inflammation can be demonstrated by one
or more of the following:
Sputum Eosinophils 3% or more
FENO of 50 ppb or more
Eosinophil count of 0.3X109/L or higher
Prompt deterioration of asthma control after a 25% or less reduction
in inhaled corticosteroid dose
Studies have shown an association between higher levels of FENO and
eosinophilic airway inflammation, although the mechanism by which this
occurs is still unclear.
Option A - the correct answer
Option B - there is insufficient evidence to support a diagnosis of allergic
bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) and therefore a course of
voriconazole is not indicated
Option C - Another advantage of mepolizumab if that is has been shown
to improve asthma symptoms to such an extent that steroid-dependent
patients can actually cease their oral corticosteroid therapy. Given the
significant side effects long-term corticosteroid therapy can have,
increasing the steroid dose further is not the most appropriate
management step, especially when there is a treatment that specifically
targets this patient's asthma phenotype
Option D - home nebulisers would not treat the underlying problem of
eosinophilic asthma
Option E - There is no indication for HRCT in this case.

A 64-year-old woman was brought in by ambulance following an out-of-
hospital cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved
with 2 cycles of resuscitation. She has spent the following 3 days in the
intensive care unit, intubated and ventilated.
On the morning round, it is noted that she is requiring a higher fraction of
inspired oxygen to maintain normal saturations and is bringing up
copious amounts of secretions. A sample of sputum is sent for
microscopy, culture, and sensitivity (MC&S). These results are shown
below:
Sputum MC&S
Bacteroides fragilis
What is the most likely explanation for these results?
Aspiration pneumonia
Contaminated sample
Hospital-acquired pneumonia
Seeding of bacteraemia
Ventilator-associated pneumonia
Question 121 of 140
A 64-year-old woman was brought in by ambulance following an out-of-
hospital cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved
with 2 cycles of resuscitation. She has spent the following 3 days in the
intensive care unit, intubated and ventilated.
On the morning round, it is noted that she is requiring a higher fraction of
inspired oxygen to maintain normal saturations and is bringing up
copious amounts of secretions. A sample of sputum is sent for
microscopy, culture, and sensitivity (MC&S). These results are shown
below:
Sputum MC&S
Bacteroides fragilis
What is the most likely explanation for these results?
explanation:
This woman is suffering from aspiration pneumonia, likely secondary to
her cardiac arrest. Not only does this fit the clinical history, but the
anaerobic growth (Bacteroides fragilis) on MC&S provides further
evidence that this is the case. This is therefore the most likely answer.
Anaerobic bacteria in sputum culture suggest aspiration pneumonia
A contaminated sample may be suspected if the MC&S grows a bacteria
that does not fit the clinical picture, however, Bacteroides fragilis is rarely
a contaminant and its presence is consistent with the clinical picture
here. The most common contaminants are coagulase-negative
staphylococci species in blood cultures.
A hospital-acquired pneumonia could explain this clinical picture
however the distinguishing feature is the sputum MC&S. Bacteroides
fragilis is an anaerobe associated with aspiration pneumonia, making
hospital-acquired pneumonia less likely.
Secondary seeding of a Bacteroides fragilis bacteraemia is less likely
than aspiration in this instance given the clinical history of cardiac arrest
and no mention of further systemic features on infection. Further blood
cultures to investigate this possibility would be a reasonable further step
to take.
As with hospital-acquired pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia
is less likely than aspiration pneumonia here due to the species grown.
Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobe associated with aspiration
pneumonia.
Aspiration pneumonia
Aspiration pneumonia is a pneumonia that develops as a result of
foreign materials gaining entry to the bronchial tree, usually oral or
gastric contents such as food and saliva. Depending on the acidity of the
aspirate a chemical pneumonitis can develop, as well as bacterial
pathogens adding to the inflammation.
Aspiration pneumonia often results from an incompetent swallowing
mechanism, such as those that occur in neurological disease or injury
such as stroke, multiple sclerosis and intoxication. Iatrogenic causes,

had COPD for five years and is on regular bronchodilator treatment with
a combination budesonide and formoterol fumarate inhaler and
salbutamol inhaler as needed. He has found that he suffers from regular
coughing bouts and finds his exercise tolerance has reduced.
His past medical history includes macular degeneration, osteoarthritis,
mild memory impairment and diverticulosis. He has noticed that the
distance he can walk has reduced from being able to go to the local
shop, roughly one mile away, to having to stop half-way to catch his
breath.
What investigation would be most useful to help determine the severity
of his COPD?
FEV1/FVC
Chest X-ray
High resolution CT scan of the chest
Partial pressure of oxygen on arterial blood gas
FEV1% of predicted
Question 122 of 140
A 72-year-old gentleman presents for review in the medical clinic. He has
had COPD for five years and is on regular bronchodilator treatment with
a combination budesonide and formoterol fumarate inhaler and
salbutamol inhaler as needed. He has found that he suffers from regular
coughing bouts and finds his exercise tolerance has reduced.
His past medical history includes macular degeneration, osteoarthritis,
mild memory impairment and diverticulosis. He has noticed that the
distance he can walk has reduced from being able to go to the local
shop, roughly one mile away, to having to stop half-way to catch his
breath.
What investigation would be most useful to help determine the severity
of his COPD?
options: High resolution CT scan of the chest
Partial pressure of oxygen on arterial blood gas
explanation:
The correct answer is FEV1% of predicted. All of the mentioned
investigations, in addition to routine blood tests, can be useful in
assessing COPD, but the primary investigation standard for COPD is
FEV1% of predicted. This compares the patient's ability to exhale over
one second with what someone of the same sex, height, weight and
ethnicity. It is a marker of the extent of airway obstruction and therefore
a marker of COPD severity.
FEV1/FVC is useful in diagnosis but not the severity of COPD.
Imaging can show radiological changes, but these are not as
standardised as spirometry changes.
Hypoxia on arterial blood gases is more useful in establishing the need
for home oxygen than COPD severity.

A 60-year-old woman is referred to the general respiratory clinic with
increasing shortness of breath over the last nine month months. This
has been associated with pedal oedema. There is no orthopnoea,
paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or cough. Her past medical history
includes bilateral extensive pulmonary emboli and she is currently taking
warfarin. She has no other lung disease and she does not smoke.
On examination her chest is clear but auscultation demonstrates a loud
second heart sound. There is also a right ventricular heave with visible V-
waves on jugular venous pressure.
A recent CT pulmonary angiogram showed resolution of the thrombus.
Echocardiogram demonstrates severe right heart dilatation and impaired
function with moderate tricuspid regurgitation.
What test will most likely provide a formal diagnosis?
Cardiac MR imaging
Right heart catheterisation
Left heart catheterisation
Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) measurement
6-minute walk test
Question 124 of 140
A 60-year-old woman is referred to the general respiratory clinic with
increasing shortness of breath over the last nine month months. This
has been associated with pedal oedema. There is no orthopnoea,
paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea or cough. Her past medical history
includes bilateral extensive pulmonary emboli and she is currently taking
warfarin. She has no other lung disease and she does not smoke.
On examination her chest is clear but auscultation demonstrates a loud
second heart sound. There is also a right ventricular heave with visible V-
waves on jugular venous pressure.
A recent CT pulmonary angiogram showed resolution of the thrombus.
Echocardiogram demonstrates severe right heart dilatation and impaired
function with moderate tricuspid regurgitation.
What test will most likely provide a formal diagnosis?
explanation:
This lady has right sided heart failure. The most likely diagnosis is
chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and she requires a
right heart catheterization to assess the pulmonary pressures
(pulmonary hypertension = pulmonary arterial pressure 25 mmHg). Note
these can be estimated on echocardiogram and cardiac MR imaging but
should not be used to formally diagnose the condition. A cardiac MR can
be used to further assess the right ventricular volumes, mass and
function or for longitudinal follow up of patients treated for pulmonary
hypertension.
A left heart catheterization is used to assess the coronary arteries and
left side of the heart which should be relatively normal in this lady.
The BNP will invariably be raised given the severe right ventricular
impairment and dilatation.
The 6-minute walk test is used as a prognostic measurement in
pulmonary hypertension.
Further reading:
Badesch DB, Champion HC, Sanchez MAG et al. Diagnosis and
assessment of pulmonary arterial hypertension. JACC 2009;54:S5566.

A 54-year-old woman is reviewed in gastroenterology clinic following the
insertion of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). She
is known to have alcohol related hepatic cirrhosis with portal
hypertension and was found to have large varices on endoscopy and
therefore underwent the insertion of a TIPS two months ago. However,
she has started to feel breathless in the last month and found that her
exercise tolerance has been reduced. She has otherwise felt well and
denies any pain, confusion or nausea. On examination, there is evidence
of chronic liver disease including palmar erythema, Dupuytren's
contracture, spider naevi and leukonychia. Her chest is clear on
auscultation. There is a loud P2 sound but otherwise, there are no
abnormalities on cardiac auscultation. What is the most likely cause of
breathlessness?
Hepatorenal syndrome
Pulmonary hypertension
Anaemia
Pleural effusion
COPD
Question 126 of 140
A 54-year-old woman is reviewed in gastroenterology clinic following the
insertion of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS). She
is known to have alcohol related hepatic cirrhosis with portal
hypertension and was found to have large varices on endoscopy and
therefore underwent the insertion of a TIPS two months ago. However,
she has started to feel breathless in the last month and found that her
exercise tolerance has been reduced. She has otherwise felt well and
denies any pain, confusion or nausea. On examination, there is evidence
of chronic liver disease including palmar erythema, Dupuytren's
contracture, spider naevi and leukonychia. Her chest is clear on
auscultation. There is a loud P2 sound but otherwise, there are no
abnormalities on cardiac auscultation. What is the most likely cause of
breathlessness?
explanation:
The correct answer is pulmonary hypertension. This is a known
complication of TIPS as the procedure causes an increased cardiac
preload by diverting blood past the cirrhotic liver, thereby significantly
reducing peripheral resistance. This can lead to pulmonary hypertension
which can explain the patient's breathlessness. The absence of
respiratory findings makes pleural effusion and COPD unlikely. With
effusions, dullness and reduced air entry would be expected and COPD
could occur with cirrhosis in anti-trypsin deficiency, but the absence of
wheeze makes this very unlikely. Anaemia can occur, but is unlikely to be
related to TIPS.

for no more than one hour. Patients with COPD can develop community
acquired pneumonia (CAP) with metabolic acidosis due to the sepsis,
but in these cases NIV is not indicated.
This patient presented with CAP and he had metabolic acidosis. His
CURB65 score is 3 and he also has acute kidney injury. He should be
treated with intravenous fluids, intravenous antibiotics, nebulisers and
steroids but not NIV.

A 41-year-old woman is seen in the respiratory clinic with a 4-month
history of a productive cough and shortness of breath on exertion. There
is no history of fever or weight loss although she does describe feeling
more fatigued. Her past medical history includes coeliac disease and
she smokes 10 cigarettes/day.
Her observations are recorded as follows:
Temperature 36.1ºC
Heart rate 87bpm
Blood pressure 114/67mmHg
Respiratory rate 15 breaths/min
Saturations 94% on room air
On examination, there is evidence of finger clubbing. On auscultation,
bilateral coarse crackles are heard. Heart sounds are normal and her
abdominal examination is unremarkable.
A high resolution computed tomography (HRCT) chest is requested:
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis here is bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis is the term given to
a respiratory condition characterised by the permanent dilatation of the
airways. This transverse slice of a CT chest shows multiple dilated
bronchi, in keeping with the diagnosis. Causes of bronchiectasis include
chronic infection and inflammation for example cystic fibrosis or
following treatment for mycobacterium tuberculosis. This patient has
had recurrent respiratory tract infections which may be involved in the
pathogenesis of bronchiectasis in this patient. Symptoms include a
persistent productive cough, shortness of breath and haemoptysis.
Coarse crackles may be heard on auscultation and finger clubbing may
be present.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a bacterial infection characterised by
fever, lethargy and a productive cough. Constitutional symptoms such as
weight loss and night sweats may also be seen. Whilst chronic
inflammation secondary to Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a cause of
bronchiectasis it is unlikely to be the current diagnosis as this patient
has no history of fever or constitutional symptoms.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is most commonly
secondary to tobacco use and a history of regular smoking can increase
the likelihood of the disease. Examination findings tend to include
wheeze rather than coarse crackles and COPD is not a cause of finger
clubbing, suggesting an alternative diagnosis. Findings in keeping with
COPD on a CT scan vary from person to person and include features
such as bronchial wall thickening, air-space enlargement and bullae
formation.
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia is a serious fungal infection
characterised by fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain and
fatigue. It is most commonly seen in patients with immunosuppression.
Autoimmune conditions are associated with coeliac disease, but coeliac
disease itself should not give rise to significant immunosuppression.
Pulmonary fibrosis presents as progressive shortness of breath and a
dry cough. It is also a cause of finger clubbing. Pulmonary fibrosis can
be diagnosed on a CT scan by the presence of the characteristic
honeycomb appearance which is not seen here.

A 75-year-old man with a background of chronic kidney disease,
hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents to the Emergency
Department with cough and breathlessness on minimal exertion. On
examination, he has bilateral inspiratory crepitations and bilateral pitting
oedema up to his sacrum. His chest radiograph shows a moderate right-
sided effusion and smaller left-sided effusion.
What single management would be most appropriate?
explanation:
This patient presents with signs and symptoms of fluid overload,
possibly due to worsening chronic kidney disease. While he has bilateral
pleural effusions, they are most likely transudative and initial
management should be to offload with IV diuretics such as furosemide.
This may lead to the resolution of his fluid overload and pleural
effusions.
Fluid restriction to 1-1.5L daily would be appropriate as part of medical
In the assessment of a pleural effusions, if the clinical picture
suggests a transudate, then you should treat the cause initially. If
this does not resolve the effusion then perform a diagnostic
aspiration
management. It should be recommended alongside diuresis with
medication as on its own it would not lead to significant offloading in a
patient who is significantly fluid overloaded.
Oral spironolactone is a diuretic that would help to offload the patient.
However, it is not commonly used as a first-line diuretic in a patient who
is significantly fluid overloaded. It also cannot be given intravenously.
Intravenous diuresis may be clinically more effective as patients who are
significantly fluid overloaded may also have gut oedema and thus have
poor absorption of oral diuretics.
The patient may need to eventually be referred for dialysis if they have
end-stage renal disease. However, many patients with chronic kidney
disease may be safely treated with diuretics without their renal function
significantly worsening. IV diuresis should thus be attempted first.
Should this fail, a renal physician could be consulted for advice,
including regarding dialysis.
Therapeutic aspiration of the larger right-sided effusion involves
aspirating up to 1.5L of fluid or inserting a chest drain to reduce the size
of the effusion. This may relieve symptoms but would be unlikely to lead
to the resolution of the contralateral effusion or improvement of this
patient's peripheral oedema. If there are atypical features, or the patient
has failed to respond to treatment such as with IV diuretics, he can be
referred for therapeutic aspiration.

A 61-year-old man with known lung cancer presents to the emergency
department with shortness of breath. He was diagnosed with squamous
cell lung cancer two years ago and has had several courses of
radiotherapy but stopped as he was not tolerating the treatment. He has
noticed worsening of his chronic shortness of breath and struggled to
walk from his car to the hospital, a distance that he was managing well
previously. On examination, he appears slightly pale, has dullness on
right side of his chest with a few bronchial breaths. A chest X-ray
demonstrates an effusion and an aspirate withdraws 40ml of blood. His
observations show hypoxia with saturations at 91% but are otherwise
normal, and blood tests, including a crossmatch, is requested. What is
the most appropriate management?
explanation:
The correct answer is a surgical chest drain. The key in this question is
that blood, rather than blood-stained fluid, is aspirated. This means that
a surgical chest drain rather than a narrow bore chest drain, a Seldinger
chest drain, will be needed. Repeating the aspiration is unlikely to gain
any further information, and would only be useful if it is suspected that
the sample was due to aspiration of an artery. However, it is unlikely that
40ml could have been aspirated from an artery. There is no indication for
antibiotics and treatment is clearly needed as the patient is hypoxic.

explanation:
The clinical scenario is of acute bronchitis in an otherwise well man.
This is usually a self-limiting condition which resolves without antibiotics
within 3 weeks and therefore the best management strategy is adequate
analgesia and hydration. Cough medicines are not routinely
recommended by NICE as they suppress natural mechanisms to keep
the airways clear.
In someone who has a chronic chest condition, antibiotics may be
prescribed but a delayed prescription strategy should be considered.
Finally, it is important to always remember to provide smoking cessation
advice.
