explanation:
Chlamydia psittaci is the correct answer. This organism can cause
Psittacosis, which is a cause of atypical pneumonia. The prodrome can
involve diarrhoea, epistaxis and high fevers. Splenomegaly and a low
white blood cell count are common. This organism should be suspected
in cases of respiratory infection together with splenomegaly and
epistaxis, which is rare as a constellation of symptoms. The classic
zoonotic exposure for this condition is birds (including parrots).
Klebsiella pneumoniae is incorrect. This is common in those people who
drink to excess, as this patient does. However, it tends to cause
cavitating pneumonia and is not associated with epistaxis.
Legionella pneumophilia is incorrect. This can cause atypical pneumonia
and diarrhoea. However, the white cell count will be elevated and it tends
not to cause epistaxis and splenomegaly is less common. Sodium may
be low and liver function may be deranged. Patients are typically
exposed to poorly ventilated air conditioning systems.
Chlamydia psittaci is a cause of atypical pneumonia. It is
transmitted via aerosol inhalation of faecal and urinary products on
bird feathers
deranged liver function. While freshwater swimming may expose the
patient to this organism, it does not cause atypical pneumonia.
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. This causes typical cavitating
pneumonia. Often this occurs as a secondary bacterial infection after an
episode of influenza.

prescribed numerous courses of antibiotics and steroids but these had
had little benefit. She was a non-smoker, did not drink alcohol and was
on no regular medications. The cough was productive of purulent
sputum with occasional streaks of blood. There was no history of weight
loss or fever, but the patient did note lethargy. The rest of her family were
well and the only medical history of note was an episode of pneumonia
as a child.
Respiratory examination revealed bilateral crackles but no other added
sounds. You note that the patient was not clubbed.
A chest x-ray, organised by the GP, shows minor bilateral atelectasis and
opacities.
What is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
options: Genetic testing for Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia
High resolution CT scan of chest
explanation:
The history is highly suggestive of bronchiectasis, which often presents
as a lower respiratory tract infection with a productive cough. Patents
may also present with haemoptysis, chest pain and shortness of breath.
Over time the condition can progress to respiratory failure.
The most common findings on examination are crackles (75%) and
wheeze (22%). Clubbing is only found in 2%.
A chest x-ray should be performed in all suspected cases and, indeed,
anyone presenting with a chronic cough. In some cases a suggestive
history and chest x-ray will be enough to diagnose bronchiectasis.
However, the best diagnostic test for bronchiectasis is high-resolution
CT scan (HRCT). A HRCT will show the classic features of bronchial wall
thickening and dilatation, it may also demonstrate features that suggest
a cause for the underlying cause, e.g. allergic bronchopulmonary
aspergillosis (ABPA) of cystic fibrosis (CF).
The routine work up for patients with suspected bronchiectasis should
include bloods for serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis,
total IgE and skin prick testing or serum IgE testing to Aspergillus
species. Bronchoscopy is not performed routinely unless there is a
suspicion of a lesion or foreign body. α1-Antitrypsin levels are not
routinely requested but may be of help if the HRCT shows evidence of
emphysema. A tuberculin skin test is very unlikely to be helpful in a
patient of this age and is not the test of choice. Tuberculin skin tests can
identify cases of latent tuberculosis but must be interpreted with the
patients immunisation history.
Genetic testing, although potentially diagnostic, would not be
appropriate in this case. Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia is an autosomal
recessive disorder that can cause bronchiesctasis but patients usually
present as newborns or in childhood and not in the elderly.

A 66-year-old man, presented with two episodes of mild haemoptysis in
the past 3 months. He also had lost 5 kilograms of weight in the past 3
months. He was a smoker with 50 pack years history and a social
drinker. He was actively mobile and had no significant past medical
history.
Clinical examination revealed no abnormality except clubbing.
A contrast enhanced CT chest showed a 4 cm mass in the right upper
lobe periphery close to the chest wall and enlarged right hilar (2 cm) and
subcarinal (2 cm) lymph nodes. A positron emission tomography (PET)
scan was done which showed a standard uptake value (SUV) max of 20
for the lung mass. The ipsilateral hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes were
also found to be FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) avid. There was no evidence
of distant metastasis.
What is the next appropriate step in the management?
CT guided biopsy of the lung mass
Ultrasound guided biopsy of the lung mass
Flexible bronchoscopic biopsy of the lung mass
Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) guided mediastinal lymph
node sampling
Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) biopsy of the
mediastinal lymph nodes

What is the next appropriate step in the management?
options: CT guided biopsy of the lung mass
Ultrasound guided biopsy of the lung mass
Flexible bronchoscopic biopsy of the lung mass
Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) guided mediastinal lymph node sampling
Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) biopsy of the mediastinal lymph nodes
explanation:
This is probably a stage IIIA (T2aN2M0) lung cancer. Diagnosis and
staging has to be confirmed by tissue sampling. EBUS guided
mediastinal lymph node sampling provides diagnosis and staging in a
single step whereas CT guided or ultrasound guided or bronchoscopic
biopsy of the lung mass yields only tissue diagnosis (not staging).
Wherever possible minimally invasive procedures should be undertaken
first for mediastinal node sampling (e.g., EBUS) before embarking into
more invasive procedures like VATS.
Reference: ESMO Consensus Guidelines: Locally-advanced stage III non-
small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
